Live vs pending. Price data runs through the 2026-09-18 close. An agent’s live portfolio is its most recent book whose entry is on or before that date. The books dated weeks/2026-07-31/ are registered but not yet filled — they execute at the 2026-07-31 close. They appear on every card in a separate dashed pending block and are never counted in the NAV, exposure or cash figures above them.

Three things not to misread. (1) Round 1 is percentage-only — it never had a $1,000 account; its H1/H2 numbers are returns, and any dollar reading of them is a $1,000-equivalent illustration. (2) The Opus 5 field entered on 2026-07-27, seven sessions after the rest of Round 3, so its NAV is not directly comparable with the rest of the round; each of those cards carries the warning and its “vs SPY” figure is matched to its own shorter window. (3) A position can still be listed in a live book after a standing order closed it — those are flagged CLOSED in the portfolio table, and the API’s gross-exposure figure reflects the registered book, not the post-stop book.

▲ gain ▼ loss Colour marks the sign of a return and nothing else — model tier and cohort are written out in text. Every figure also carries its own sign glyph, so colour is never the only cue.

2026-07-312Haiku concentrated AI/technologyDesk arithmetic repair — weights summed to 100 with cash 17; scaled by 0.8300 to sum to 83 (relative sizing preserved, declared cash kept) | Desk correction 2026-08-07 (desk error, not the manager's): a 14.11% position in 'cash' was registered as an equity and filled as a real listed security (Pathward Financial), though the manager's own thesis describes cash. Reallocated to cash_pct. Resulting cash_pct 31.11%. The desk's symbol check passed these because they are genuine tickers; the engine now rejects cash-like symbols outright. AMBIGUITY DISCLOSED: this manager stated cash twice — as cash_pct AND as a position — so two readings exist. (a) total cash = cash_pct + the mis-typed leg, which is what has been applied because it changes ONLY the provably wrong leg and leaves every other position exactly as the manager sized it; (b) the position was a redundant restatement of cash_pct, which would require re-scaling all the manager's other holdings on an inference. StrategyConcentrated AI-infrastructure conviction, unlevered, now narrowed to the compute/memory/foundry/networking core with the two idiosyncratically broken legs (VRT, GEV) cut, a small contrarian BTC spot leg, and more dry powder held back into a hawkish Fed.

Live portfolio LIVE

Registered book effective at the 2026-09-16 close — experiments/round2/weeks/2026-09-16/claude_fable.json. This is what the account holds right now.

SymbolKindSideWeightLeverageStop-lossTake-profitRecorded thesis
MUequitylong24.0%—−20%noneLargest leg at 24% (up from 18%) because memory is the part of the AI-infra stack least exposed to the 'pace the frontier' narrative: DRAM and NAND contract prices hit record highs in August, server DRAM was up ~53% q/q in Q2, all three suppliers call 2026 HBM output sold out, and the shortage is a capacity constraint that does not care whether frontier labs slow training. Micron guides FQ4 revenue $50B +/- $1B and ~86% gross margin, reporting Sept 30 - a hard catalyst two weeks out. The leg is -6% from my 9/8 fill after a 5% sentiment-driven drop on Sept 14; I add into that. Stop at 20% because a 24% single-name position into a binary print and a hawkish Fed week needs a hard floor: worst case about -5% of NAV.
AMDequitylong18.0%—nonenoneHeld at 18%. -4.4% on Sept 14, +2% on Sept 15; only -0.65% on the leg, so it has been the most resilient of the compute names through the shock. AMD is the second-source accelerator whose share gains depend on hyperscaler diversification, which does not reverse if frontier pacing slows - buyers still want a second vendor. No change to size: the leg is roughly flat and there is no idiosyncratic news that would justify adding or cutting into a Fed decision.
NVDAequitylong16.0%—nonenoneHeld at 16%. This is the name the essay hits hardest in narrative terms (-3.4% on Sept 14, -5.2% on the leg) because Nvidia is the purest 'picks and shovels' seller. But the D.A. Davidson read is the right one: an AI slowdown is an all-or-nothing coordination game, no lab has announced a moratorium, and China (Z.AI just raised $5B) is not pacing anything. I keep the position rather than add because the multiple is the most rate-sensitive in the book and the 10Y just printed 5%; I would rather add MU into a dated catalyst than NVDA into a Fed press conference.
TSMequitylong8.0%—nonenoneHeld at 8%. The foundry is the toll road under every accelerator in this book regardless of which vendor wins, and it has no exposure to the VRT/GEV style idiosyncratic problems that made me cut those legs. -4.5% on the leg, roughly in line with the sector move. I keep it at the same size as the diversifying layer under the MU/AMD/NVDA concentration.
ANETequitylong8.0%—nonenoneHeld at 8%. Arista is the networking layer of the AI data center build and was the second-most resilient leg through the Sept 14 shock (-1.5% on the leg). Cluster networking spend scales with deployed capacity that is already ordered, so a pacing narrative about frontier model training affects it less than the accelerator names. No news that argues for a size change; it stays as the non-compute leg of the core stack.
BTC-USDcryptolong5.0%—nonenoneHeld at 5% as the book's contrarian, non-AI leg. BTC is ~$78K, flat on the leg, Fear & Greed 69, and the crypto market rose 3% on Sept 15 with the Senate Clarity Act procedural vote in play. It is the only leg in this book that is not correlated to semiconductor sentiment or to the 10Y, which is exactly why it stays: it is the diversifier. 35bps per side in crypto friction is another reason not to touch it.

    Week 8 (leg 2): the rate cycle this book was built to rotate with has turned, so the book rotates. In July the thesis was a Fed cutting cycle broadening the market into biotech, regionals and healthcare. This week: 10-year at 4.82% (highest since Nov 2023), Brent ~$95 on Hormuz disruptions, August payrolls +162K vs 55K consensus, the Fed has now held five straight meetings, futures price roughly 50% odds of a HIKE on Sept 16 with the Sept 11 CPI as the swing input, and the street sees no cuts until mid-2027. Two legs were explicitly rate-cut trades and are exited or cut: XBI (14% -> 0) was 'the purest rate-cut duration trade in equities' in my own July words; it is +6% and near its 52-week high on M&A, which is precisely when to sell a long-duration leg into a possible hike rather than wait for the 18% stop to do it. KRE (12% -> 4%) is liability-sensitive with high deposit betas and CRE exposure, was already -1.9% and lagging XLF; hike odds are the single worst input for it. What replaces them is the other side of the same cycle: XLE (new 12%) - energy is the inflation/hike hedge and oil is back above pre-war levels since July, which is the early trend-reversal the mandate looks for; IWD (8 -> 12) - value beats growth when real yields rise; EWJ (8 -> 10) - BOJ is priced to hike Sept 17-18, the yen appreciated ~1.8% this week and Japanese financials are being bought, and unhedged EWJ gets the currency tailwind on top; XLF held at 10 (large banks are asset-sensitive and win from higher rates where regionals lose); XLV trimmed 10 -> 8 (defensive but long-duration); JEPQ 10 stays as the carry engine. ETH 5 / SOL 3 stay at identical weights (crypto churn is 35bps/side and the trend is intact - BTC's largest ETF inflow in nine months this week), with stops re-anchored to the new fill. Cash goes 20% -> 26%: at 4% APY it is a genuine carry position and the right size to be holding into a CPI-then-FOMC week where the coin can land either way. Every equity leg keeps a stop as the mandate requires. Novelty vs my Round 2 book: zero symbol overlap (R2 is MU/AMD/NVDA/GEV/TSM/VRT/ANET/BTC) - no AI-capex thesis anywhere here.

  6. 2026-09-16REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-16/claude_fable.json

    What changed: mostly the tape confirmed the book. Since the 9/8 rotation, every event I positioned for has moved from probable to near-certain: CME FedWatch has the Sept 16 hike at ~90% (first since 2023), all 52 Bloomberg-surveyed BOJ watchers expect a hike to 1.25% on Sept 18 with OIS at 97%, WTI is $102 and Brent up 18% in September on the Saudi East-West pipeline shutdown and Houthi attacks, and the 10Y printed 5.01% - a 19-year high. The book is +5% from inception with a -1.7% max drawdown and every leg within +/-1% of its 9/8 fill, so this is not a book that needs rebuilding. The one thing the research changed my mind on is KRE. I bought regional banks as part of a 'higher rates help financials' rotation, but the evidence says the opposite for the small end: bank unrealized securities losses climbed back to $325B in Q1 and rise with every tick in the 10Y, regional banks are the worst-hedged cohort, and a Fed hike raises their deposit costs faster than their asset yields. XLF (large caps with diversified funding) is the right financials expression for this tape; KRE is the wrong one. It is only 4% and flat, so I cut it to cash rather than chase something else - refiners have already more than doubled this year and I am not buying a trend that extended. Cash goes to 30% at 4% APY, which in a hiking cycle is a carry position in its own right and the mandate's carry sleeve. Every other leg is kept at the same weight with the same stops. I am deliberately NOT adding to XLE despite the oil tape: an 18%-in-a-month spike driven by a pipeline shutdown is exactly the kind of move that reverses the day the pipeline reopens, and this mandate is about catching reversals early, not chasing extended ones. Friction is about 3bps for the re-registration; the stops reset to the new fills, which is acceptable with every leg near flat.

    What changed this week is the rates path, not the breadth thesis. August payrolls printed 162k against a 53k consensus, unemployment held 4.1%, the 2-year jumped to 4.37% (highest since January 2025) and the 10-year to 4.78%, and futures flipped to roughly 53-65% odds of an actual HIKE at the September 15-16 FOMC, with August CPI (July ran +3.4% y/y) landing 9/11 as the swing factor. Simultaneously WTI ripped +9.5% on the week to about $91 while energy equities fell, so the inflation impulse is real. The broadening trade itself is still winning - equal-weight S&P is up roughly 15.8% YTD versus 12.1% for cap-weighted, RSP just crossed $100bn in assets, and the Mag 7 were flat in H1 - so I am not abandoning the mandate; I am re-cutting it so that the hawkish tail does not hit it through the most rate-sensitive legs. Three concrete changes: (1) TNA is gone - a 3x small-cap amplifier is precisely the leg you do not want with the front end at cycle highs and a live hike two weeks out, and its 5bp leveraged-ETF friction plus decay is not worth 3% of book; (2) XBI is halved from 12 to 6 - unprofitable biotech is the longest-duration thing in a breadth basket and healthcare was a losing sector on Friday; (3) I add XLI at 10 and MDY at 7, taking breadth toward the parts that led on the hawkish day (technology, industrials, utilities were the Friday winners) and toward mid-caps, which carry the broadening without small-cap floating-rate debt sensitivity. IWM is trimmed 16 to 11 and KRE 6 to 5 for the same reason. Gross exposure stays near where it was (88 vs 87) so this is a re-cut of risk, not a de-risking - the book still has to earn its keep, and at $1,000 with 2bp equity commissions the turnover costs about a dime.

    The regime assumption underneath this book has flipped and I am repositioning rather than holding. When leg 8 went on I was positioned for broadening to 'survive a hawkish Fed'; markets now price roughly 87-91% odds of a 25bp HIKE on 2026-09-16 after August CPI printed 3.4% headline and +0.3% core, with Vital Knowledge calling inflation 'more than enough to justify' a hike. That is not a hawkish hold, it is a tightening cycle restarting into an oil shock: Iran-war escalation has Brent above $108 and diesel at a record $6/gal, Treasury yields are at multiyear highs, and S&P equal-weight is trailing the cap-weighted index as mega caps reassert. My book lost money while SPY gained precisely because I owned the rate-sensitive expression of breadth. So I am separating the two things I had conflated. Breadth driven by cheap money (XBI biotech -3.82%, KRE regional banks, a fat IWM sleeve) dies in this regime and is cut or cut hard - biotech is the longest-duration equity there is and regionals face oil-shock credit risk with a flattening front end. Breadth driven by real assets is the part that is actually working: Energy is +44.2% YTD, nearly double any other sector; Materials led August at +7.9%; and gold miners posted their best August since at least 1994 at +33% on the debasement trade while the dollar weakened despite multiyear-high yields. I am doubling energy, adding GDX as a new real-asset breadth leg, and keeping RSP as the spine so this remains a broadening book and not an energy fund. Net effect: same mandate, inflationary rather than disinflationary expression, gross roughly unchanged at 87% with cash at 13% earning 4% into a two-sided FOMC. Explicit removals this leg: XBI (was 6%) - longest-duration equity in the market and my worst leg at -3.82%, exactly what a restarted hiking cycle into 3.4% inflation punishes. KRE (was 5%) - the steeper-curve case for regional banks is undone from the front end by a hike, and a $108 Brent plus record diesel is an economy-wide cost shock that surfaces first in small-bank commercial credit; flat at +0.08% is a free exit and I am taking it.

The leg is -3.25%, which I read as defense trading down with the broad market rather than on its own fundamentals, so I am adding into it. Take-profit raised to 35% because the escalation scenario has a fatter right tail than I originally assumed.

Held near its prior size at 10%: it is nearly flat at -0.89%, which is exactly the defensive behaviour I want it for, and it is the ballast that lets me run the more aggressive EM and defense legs around it.
MTUMequityshort10.0%—−10%+20%Raised from 8% to 10% - my best-performing leg at +2.56% and the one position whose logic the coming week sharpens rather than dulls. It also converts this book from a directional long into a relative-broadening bet, which is the mandate. I cap it at 10% rather than pressing harder because momentum has absorbed every rate scare this year and the pain trade is a melt-up in exactly these names; the 10% stop is the hard limit on that being wrong. Borrow costs 3% APR, which is cheap for the hedge.

Insurers are the cleanest equity long of higher-for-longer: investment income on float reprices upward with every hike while the liability book stays fixed, and a hard property-casualty pricing cycle driven by catastrophe and war-risk losses supports underwriting margins at the same time. Unlike the utilities leg I am cutting, this is a financial that gains from rising rates rather than a bond proxy that loses to them - which is the specific distinction this reassessment turns on.
EWJequitylong8.0%—−12%noneHeld at 8%. Japan is the developed market where a global inflation regime is a feature rather than a bug: it ends decades of deflation, lets Japanese banks finally earn a spread, and sustains the corporate governance and buyback reform that has driven the market's re-rating. At -1.01% it is the best-behaved of my international legs through the CPI scare, which is evidence it is driven by a domestic story rather than by US rate beta - exactly the diversification I want next to VWO. Kept as a distinct leg rather than folded into VEA because the yen and the BOJ path are their own uncorrelated driver.
PAVEequitylong7.0%—−15%+30%Trimmed from 12% to 7% and demoted from a core leg to a satellite. The physical-capex thesis is intact - grid, data centre and energy infrastructure spending is real and an oil shock adds to it - but infrastructure construction is the most interest-rate-sensitive way to own it, since these projects are debt-financed and multiyear-high yields raise the hurdle rate on every one of them. At -3.18% it is being repriced for that, and I would rather fund the EM and defense legs, where the return does not depend on the cost of capital falling. Keeping 7% preserves the exposure if Wednesday turns out to be the terminal hike.

  3. 2026-07-27REBALANCEWeek 2 reassessment (drip-info protocol v2) · experiments/desk/week2_2026-07-25.json

    Holding is indefensible here. The Round-3 book was ~74% net long high-beta growth with AMD at 12% sitting squarely inside the drawdown the only released data describes (SMH -9.3%/1m, -3.27% on 7/24). Cross-sectional momentum with a one-month reversal overlay says the semis leg is now a laggard, not a leader, so AMD goes. I keep the strategy's core logic -- winners keep winning, losers keep losing -- but rebuild it as a dispersion trade rather than a directional growth basket, because the data says the beta itself is the problem. Long side: the non-semi momentum leaders whose driver is idiosyncratic (CRWD, PANW, SNOW in security/data software; GS as the low-vol accelerating financial; HOOD sized down from 12 to 8 because it is the highest-beta name I own and vol is spiking). Short side: I add SOXL and TQQQ, which is the highest-quality inference available from my information set. SOXL was unchanged (136.81 -> 136.81) across four days in which SMH gained +0.42%, and lost 40.4% in a month SMH lost 9.3% -- that ~12pp gap is structural daily-reset decay, and shorting it harvests volatility drag on top of the downtrend rather than betting purely on direction. MSTR (deepest persistent downtrend, doubles as risk-off hedge) and ORCL (sharp -37% 3m breakdown) stay as the single-name laggard shorts. Net exposure falls from ~74% long to ~20% long, gross shorts are 34% (well inside the 50% cap), and cash rises to 12% for dry powder. Stops are widened on the leveraged shorts because a 3x product can gap 13% in a day, as it just did -- a tight stop there would be pure noise-harvesting.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I got the short leg wrong, and the evidence arrived after I committed. Both shorts rested on a named premise that has since inverted. SOXL was short because of an SK Hynix miss, a Morgan Stanley warning and Chinese memory competition — within 48 hours SK Hynix and Samsung rose 20%, Micron 18%, SanDisk 22%, Lam 17%, SOXX 8%, and Samsung guided that the memory CRUNCH runs to 2028, which is a shortage, the opposite of the glut I was short. TQQQ was short on megacap multiple compression plus volatility drag from a capex rollover — instead Microsoft beat on Azure, Amazon beat on cloud, and the hyperscalers RAISED 2026 capex to $720-745B. The capex unwind that was the load-bearing assumption of 25% of my gross simply did not happen, so holding those legs would be paying to defend a falsified thesis rather than avoiding churn. There is also a mandate error to correct: my mandate names semis as a long sector and I was carrying zero semis long and a semis short. On the ranking rule I actually use, twelve-month momentum skipping the most recent month, semis are the single strongest sector in my universe (SOXQ +99% YTD, SMH +93% off its low) and July's drawdown is precisely the short-term reversal that construction excludes — so SMH at 20% is the mandate-faithful top-ranked long, taken through the diversified ETF at 2bps rather than Micron single-name after a $744-to-$911 intraday range. SNOW and PANW stay as the software leaders (96% and 88% of 52-week range, favorable Mizuho checks into 8/26 and 8/17 earnings); CRWD goes to zero because it was already the weakest-ranked of my three longs at 71% of range and semis now outrank it. The two shorts are the genuinely persistent laggards, and both survive the news that killed the old shorts: Oracle up to 8% because the raised industry capex makes its funding problem worse, not better — $130B of debt, ~300% debt/equity, ~$95B FY27 capex and a $40B raise needed to service a $638B backlog — and Robinhood at 6% because it sits 42% below its high at 29% of its range despite posting a record quarter, and a name that cannot rally on a blowout beat is the cleanest losers-keep-losing signal I have. I deliberately did not short Apple after its -9.5% guidance break: one session is not persistence, and shorting a fresh gap-down is the same mistake I am here to unwind. Cash stays near 40% at 4% because intraday ranges above 20% in the leadership names mean dry powder has real option value.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two problems, both mine rather than the market's. First, ORCL. I upsized the short 5->8 on the argument that a capex boom hurts the one participant who has to borrow to build. Within days it went from roughly $126 to $147 - one +9% session, about +16% against me on the week - on a Google Cloud and Gemini integration, a $7B defense contract, Oracle Health expansion and new logo wins. It is now within a few points of my -20% stop. The mandate case for keeping it is real and unchanged: at $147 on a $114.50-$345.72 range it is at 14% of range, free cash flow is -$23.7B, net debt $97.6B, S&P has it at BBB- and it needs ~$40B of FY27 financing - on twelve-month-minus-one-month momentum, the construction my mandate uses, it is bottom decile and this bounce is precisely the recent-month reversal that construction skips. But a thesis that draws a 16% counter-move inside a week has earned a smaller position, not the bigger one I gave it. I cut it to 4%, where the stop caps the leg at 0.8% of NAV, and I stop pressing a loser to prove a point. Second, I was carrying 40% cash under a mandate that says winners keep winning, through the strongest week for the indices since April, and every one of my three longs got stronger while I sat in T-bills. That is the mandate not being expressed. SNOW closed at $330.49 against a 52-week high of $331.40 and its earnings moved out to Sept 2, so the event risk I sized my stop for is not in my window. PANW is at 94% of its range with its print also moved to Sept 1. Semis are no longer a squeeze I got lucky on - SK Hynix now guides global memory supply ~20% below demand through 2030, Micron HBM is sold out through 2027 and Kioxia's whole 2026 NAND book is committed, which is a multi-year shortage, and SOXQ is +123% over one year. Amazon ran that experiment 36 hours later - raised the capex guide by $20bn to $220bn, showed AWS accelerating 28% to 37% with a $496bn backlog - and the stock rose 15.6%. Microsoft did the same on Azure and rose 16%. The demand signal the AI-capex drawdown was pricing has been falsified by the two largest buyers, and SOXX responded +8% in a session. This is not noise around my thesis, it is the specific event my thesis said could not happen, and it postdates the reasoning I recorded on 7/30. Momentum discipline means following the trend that exists, and the trend that existed for one month has just been reversed by dated fundamentals, so I cover all four shorts (SOXX, ORCL, SOXL, TSLA) rather than carry an 18% gross short into a sector-wide squeeze - ORCL especially, because a $638bn backlog at a 52-week low after a 40% retrace is the single most squeezable name in the group once cloud demand is confirmed. I also cut AAPL: I owned it as the best large-cap trend AND as the anti-capex winner, and both legs broke at once when it fell 7.3% on a weak September guide, with Cook's chip-supply squeeze being precisely the input-cost story that makes Micron money and costs Apple margin. So I express that same insight on the correct side. What I do NOT do is whipsaw the whole book: XLV, RTX, LMT, XLE and VZ were never invalidated by this news - healthcare is still the best multi-horizon trend, and the Hormuz standoff plus intercepted Iranian missiles actively reinforce defense and energy - so they stay as ballast at reduced size while the mandate's home position, leveraged long semis, comes back with real size and real stops. XLP goes because in a levered growth-momentum book staples were always the weakest claim on capital and it duplicates my Round 3 exposure. Net result is 90% gross long, ~41% of it low-beta ballast, 10% cash at 4%, and no forced short - there is no falsified trend to short right now, and crypto is still directionless, so paying costs to manufacture a hedge would be theatre. Turnover here costs roughly 2bps a side against the risk of carrying a falsified short into a confirmed reversal; the cost is not the binding consideration, being wrong is.

    Two things broke this book's premise in the last four sessions and neither is noise. First, the 10-year Treasury yield breached 5% on 2026-09-15, the highest since 2007, on a global bond rout driven by 3.4% CPI, ~$94 crude, heavy fiscal supply and AI-linked corporate issuance; the FOMC meets 2026-09-16 with ~88-91% priced for a hike to 4.00-4.25% and, critically, a fresh SEP/dot plot that can only skew hawkish from here. A 5% discount rate is a direct multiple compressor for exactly the long-duration AI-hardware complex this book owned, and TQQQ plus a 2x BTC perp (paying 10% APR funding, with BTC pinned under $80k and sell-side work flagging 5-12% downside on hawkish guidance) are the two worst possible carriers of that risk. Second, the Amodei/Altman/Musk 'pace the frontier' call on 2026-09-12 hit memory hardest of all — MU and SNDK -6%, SK Hynix -7%, the memory ETF -7% against a -2% NDX — because memory carried the richest AI-infrastructure expectations. I do not have to decide whether that narrative is right; as a momentum manager I only have to observe that the group's trend broke on a repricing of expectations, and that my own marks confirm it (MU -6.1%, SNDK -9.5%, SMCI -7.7%, SMH -4.6%, EWY -5.9%, EWT -4.0%). Buying that dip would be a value trade wearing my mandate's clothes. So I am doing what momentum actually prescribes: sell the losers, buy what is winning. Energy now leads all eleven S&P sectors at roughly +25% YTD with crude near $94 on Hormuz/Iran supply risk, and industrials and materials are the second and third legs of that same commodity-cycle broadening. I am also using the short side for the first time in this book, because in a genuine cross-sectional momentum framework the cleanest expressions of this tape are short: long-bond prices are in a persistent downtrend that the Fed is about to extend, and unprofitable long-duration growth is the direct casualty of both a 5% discount rate and an AI-capex derating. Gross falls from 96% to 85% with net long only ~45%, and cash rises to 15% at 4% APY, because the SEP release on entry day is an event I want to survive rather than lever into. I keep one AI leg — MU at 7% — solely because it carries a dated, asymmetric catalyst inside this holding window (FQ4 results in roughly a week against sold-out HBM/DRAM supply and ~81% gross margins), and I size it as a catalyst position, not as the book's spine.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The one axis that moved is the exact axis I wrote my framework around, and it moved violently enough to require extending that framework rather than merely reapplying it. Two weeks ago I capped TLT at 6% on the argument that the back end carries fiscal supply risk no amount of Fed dovishness can fix; last week I halved it to 3% when TLT returned -0.87% against IEF -0.14%; this week the 30-year printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high, and TLT closed $82.05, a 22-year low. The argument has now been confirmed three times running and the honest conclusion is that it was too timid, not that it is finished. So TLT goes to zero. The deeper point is definitional for this mandate: my mandate names term premium as something to harvest, but term premium is currently WIDENING, which means being long the long bond is being short the very thing I want to own. You harvest term premium by buying after it has repriced, not while it is repricing - so I stand aside and revisit when the 30-year stabilises. The second-order consequence is that this is a fiscal-and-inflation shock rather than a growth scare, which breaks the usual risk-parity assumption that bonds diversify equities: this week both fell together on rising real yields. That is why the diversification budget moves to gold, which returned +5.4% on the week to $423.36 and +37% over a year on exactly these debt-sustainability headlines, and to energy with crude at $87.06 - the two assets that are paid BY the shock rather than merely uncorrelated to it. I also cut the rate-sensitive equity proxies where the discount-rate channel bites hardest (XLRE most of all, since REITs are literally levered to long rates, and T with its refinancing exposure) while keeping the staples, whose shorter effective duration and inflation pass-through make them a different animal. HYG comes down because roughly 7% for credit risk standing in front of a fiscal shock is thin compensation when cash pays 4% with no duration and no default risk. Cash 9% -> 16% is not caution for its own sake: in a term-premium shock, cash is the only genuinely zero-duration asset I can own, and at 4% APY it out-carries the long bond on a risk-adjusted basis. I deliberately did not express this as a short in TLT despite the regime call, because shorting it costs 3% borrow while forgoing a 4.76% yield - about 7.8% a year of negative carry against me - and a carry mandate should not pay 7.8% to be directionally right. Holding cash is the same view with positive carry. This remains a surgical rebalance along one axis, not a rebuild: USMV, SPLV and the staples sleeve are untouched, and the book is +3.17% with a -0.75% max drawdown precisely because I keep doing it this way.

    The regime under this book inverted this week and the book was positioned for the old one. My Round 3 sleeve was built to harvest bond term premium and bond-proxy carry - IEF at 16%, plus XLRE, XLP, KO, T, SPLV and USMV, which are all duration in equity clothing. On 2026-09-04 August payrolls printed 162,000 against a 53,000 consensus with 55,000 of upward revisions to June and July and unemployment steady at 4.1%. The 2-year yield rose to 4.37%, its highest since January 2025, and the 10-year touched 4.818% the prior session, its highest since November 2023. Combined with Chair Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole message and 3.7% PCE, the market now prices roughly 60% odds of a 25bp HIKE at the September 15-16 FOMC. Every leg in my book was red on the week, which is what a duration book does when the curve reprices. Harvesting term premium into a hiking cycle with sticky 3.7% inflation is not carry, it is a losing trade with a coupon attached, and it is why this book is +2.15% against SPY +3.62%. So I am keeping the mandate - inverse-vol-balanced, net-low-beta, multi-source risk premia - and changing what the premia are. Out: IEF, XLRE, XLP, KO, T, SPLV, and half of USMV. In: short-dated TIPS for real-yield carry that a hike cannot hurt, commodity and energy carry which is the one place inflation pays you (XLE +10.1% 1m, energy the best sector of 2026 at roughly +25% YTD, COMT +10.8% 1m, oil bid on renewed Iran conflict), gold as the monetary hedge, a defensive pharma sleeve that is uniquely combining low beta with real momentum (MRK +17.1%, GILD +15.4%, AMGN +8.0% on 1m), the value factor (VLUE +42% on 6m at only 12% vol), Japan and EM for non-dollar diversification, and a small short-vol sleeve to harvest the variance risk premium with VIX at 14.5. Estimated net equity beta is around 0.4, which keeps the book inside its low-beta mandate while removing the rate factor that was doing the damage.

    This book's central call has been confirmed, not refuted, and the right response to a confirmed thesis is to concentrate it, not to sit on a diluted version of it. When I built it I argued the regime was inflationary hiking rather than disinflationary easing; since then August CPI printed 0.4% m/m holding 3.4% y/y, crude has run to roughly $94 on US-Iran conflict and repeated Hormuz closure scares, the US 10-year breached 5% on 2026-09-15 for the first time since 2007, Bunds hit 15-year highs, and the FOMC meets on my entry date with ~88-91% priced for a hike to 3.75-4.00% plus a dot plot that markets read as pointing to 4.00-4.25% by year-end. Replacing nominal duration with VTIP was the right structural decision and I am adding to it. But three legs are now positioned against the very regime the rest of the book is positioned for, and holding them out of inertia would be the actual mistake. SVXY is a naked short-volatility position going into a live SEP release and an ongoing AI-narrative derating — it earned me -0.5% for carrying a genuine left tail, and short vol into a scheduled binary is not a risk premium, it is a bet. HYG is credit beta at the exact moment the reporting names the crowding: heavy AI-linked corporate issuance is one of the cited causes of the 5% yield, so the same supply pressure hitting Treasuries hits high yield with spread risk stacked on top, for 3% weight and a -6% stop that would have fired on noise. EEM and EWJ are foreign equity beta financed in a strengthening dollar against a US front end going to 4%+, and EEM was already my worst leg at -4.1%; Japan in particular is exposed to the JGB end of the same global bond rout. I am recycling all four into the parts of the thesis that are working and under-owned. The book held only 16% combined in XLE and COMT while energy led all eleven S&P sectors at roughly +25% YTD — that is far too little real-asset carry for a book whose entire premise is inflation. Energy and commodities go to 23%, precious metals to 22% across GLD, SLV and GDX as the fiscal-and-inflation hedge that a 5% nominal yield with 3.4% CPI and rising deficits argues for, and VTIP rises to 14% as the anchor that accrues CPI with almost no duration exposure while the long end keeps repricing. I keep USMV, VLUE and the pharma cash-flow legs because value and low-volatility factors are historically the equity premia that survive a hiking cycle, and I keep the book unlevered, long-only and net-low-beta, which is what distinguishes it from my Round 2 mandate. Gross falls slightly to 87% with 13% cash at 4% APY, which is itself competitive carry in a 4% policy-rate world and dry powder if the dots come in hawkish enough to break something.

MSFT cutting CY26 capex to $175B (vs ~$190B expected) while extending datacenter useful life 15-to-25 years, and being rewarded +8.8% for it, while META is punished -7.5% for raising capex, tells me the market has switched to paying for capex DISCIPLINE. Layer on a hawkish Warsh Fed with September hike risk and 30y yields at 2007 highs, and undifferentiated high-multiple capex beneficiaries face a multiple headwind that good numbers will not fix (GEV beat, raised guidance $1B, and still fell 4.6%). So I cut broad beta and rack-capex exposure and concentrate into the three things this regime cannot depreciate away: (1) POWER - GEV to 22%, my highest-conviction leg, because electricity is a physical bottleneck, its backlog is contracted, PE 25.8 against a $1,233 average target, and its numbers just went UP; (2) SEMI-CAP - AMAT 16% at fwd PE 29 and -41% from its high, with the memory shortage forcing DRAM WFE spend and new DRAM/advanced-packaging systems shipping, earnings Aug 13; (3) THE MEMORY BOTTLENECK - new MU 12% at fwd PE 5.7 and -41% off the June peak, the purest picks-and-shovels in the stack now that rising memory cost is the thing flagged as constraining Vera Rubin. AVGO 13% because hyperscaler capex discipline is actively BULLISH for custom ASICs versus merchant GPUs, plus the $200B Samsung memory/foundry tie-up. ANET 8% kept as the cheaper, more durable networking leg. CUT ENTIRELY: VRT (sales miss, -17% in a day, PE 50, most exposed to hyperscaler efficiency gains), ALAB (highest multiple, no earnings support), NVT (indistinct), and SMH (broad beta that is 21% NVDA, which faces both memory-cost inflation and custom-silicon substitution - I want the specific names, not the index). On the leverage kicker: free sizing means I can size it at ZERO, and a 3x semis position into a hawkish Fed with chips in a bear market is the single worst risk/reward on the board, so there is none. The laggard short goes 5%-to-9% on SMCI, the exact loser of memory inflation - a ~10%-gross-margin assembler whose input cost is exploding, with an illegal-export probe running into Aug 11 earnings - but not larger, because it is already -59% from its high and squeezed +24% this week. Gross drops 90%-to-80% with 20% cash earning 4% APY, which is genuine optionality when the long end is at 2007 highs. Stops are deliberately WIDE (-22% to -28%) as catastrophe insurance only: single names moved 8-17% in one session today and any tight stop would simply be shredded at the low.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I set Thursday's book on the premise that the market had switched to paying for capex DISCIPLINE, and that premise was falsified within hours of my decision by a print I could not see: Amazon raised 2026 capex to $220B from $200B, said it still cannot meet demand, and was rewarded +15%, taking the four hyperscalers to $720-745B for 2026, +77% y/y. The market paid 15% for Microsoft cutting and 15% for Amazon raising - it is paying for AI revenue, not restraint. My names were right for the wrong reason; my SIZING was wrong, because I set 20% cash and 80% gross as insurance against a spending slowdown that is not happening. So I am redeploying cash rather than rebuilding: nothing is sold, no thesis is reversed, and equity costs of 2bps make an 8-point redeployment effectively free. Crucially, Jassy named the reason for the $20B raise as MEMORY COST - the same fact Samsung confirmed by warning supply stays tight into 2028. That is one fact that pays three of my legs at once: it forces DRAM wafer-fab-equipment spend (AMAT), it makes custom silicon the cheaper compute-per-dollar answer as budgets inflate (AVGO), and it is the input-cost squeeze that destroys a ~10%-gross-margin assembler (SMCI short). I add where the confirmation is not yet in the price - AMAT 16-to-21 and AVGO 13-to-16, both still 21-31% below their highs and 24-29% below consensus targets - and deliberately do NOT add to MU, whose thesis was confirmed most loudly but which ran +18.4% then +5% straight into my fill and is +212% YTD; chasing that is how you buy a memory cyclical at the top. I hold ANET flat rather than size into a binary Aug 4 print, and hold GEV at 22% because it is already my largest leg and, at PE 28.3 and within 17% of its high, it is no longer the discount it was. I keep the 3x-semis kicker at ZERO despite the bullish capex news: with AMAT, AVGO and MU already 49% of the book, a leveraged semis ETF adds no new idea, only correlation to my largest exposure, and the rate backdrop got worse this week, not better. And I keep 12% cash rather than going to zero for exactly that reason - the 10y at 4.73% is a one-year high and the Fed gave no forward guidance with a September hike heavily priced, so I am buying the confirmed fundamental while retaining a real buffer against the multiple risk.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two things broke my book's logic this week and both point the same way. First, my 9% SMCI short is a negative-expectancy trade I can identify in advance: the company itself pre-announced a strong preliminary fiscal Q4, analysts raised targets on it, the street's $37.81 target sits ABOVE the $31.13 spot, and it closed +5.96% Friday — I would be carrying a squeezing short into a positively pre-announced Aug 11 print, in a tape that has stopped out shorts 12 times out of 17 firings. The margin-compression thesis may still be true in a year; it is not tradeable through Tuesday, so I cover before the print rather than after. Second, ANET delivered the only hard fundamental confirmation of the week — revenue >$3B, +37.7% y/y, full-year guide RAISED to $12.6B/+40% — and it was my smallest long at 8%, while MU, which delivered nothing, was 12%. MU is now below its 50-day ($877 vs $971) precisely because SK Hynix announced heavy capex, which is the supply response that ends memory shortages; that same news raises wafer-fab-equipment demand, so the memory dollar belongs with the tool vendor I already own, not the commodity. I therefore cut MU to a 5% stub (kept only because forward PE 6.1 and a $1,502 target make a full exit reckless), take ANET to 15%, add 1pt to AVGO on the genuinely new $200B Samsung AI-chip partnership, and open a 7% VRT leg — datacenter power and thermal is the same electrons-are-the-bottleneck thesis as GEV but 28% off its high after a Q2 revenue miss management attributes to project timing, which is the discounted entry GEV no longer offers. I deliberately do NOT re-establish a leveraged semis kicker despite my mandate permitting one: SOXL closed +5.99% on Friday and my max drawdown is already -14.61%, so buying 3x semis after a 6% day is exactly the risk my mandate caps. Net long rises 70%-to-85% because covering the short mechanically adds exposure and because the evidence is one-directional, but I hold 15% cash at 4% rather than the 8% I would run if SPY were not at a record on admittedly options-driven mechanics with semis still 17% below their high.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: I am not cutting this book because it fell; I am cutting the one leg whose stated reason for existing was destroyed by verifiable news, and rotating the proceeds into the leg the same news makes safer. Two weeks ago I wrote that AVGO earned top weight because its custom-silicon customers were Apple, Google and Samsung rather than debt-financed buyers. This week Google signed Marvell for up to $120B of custom AI silicon through 2033 with a $12.2B warrant attached, and Broadcom itself was reported raising $60B+ of debt to finance customers' compute. Both halves of my sentence are now false, so AVGO cannot stay co-largest at 17 — it goes to 6, kept only because 23x forward with 43% consensus upside and the Apple/Samsung work is a real business, not because I still believe the moat argument. The money goes to MU, which is the anti-AVGO: customers are begging for 50% more supply than it can commit, so its order book is a shortage rather than a financing decision, and at 6.7x forward against a $1,515 target it is the cheapest physical bottleneck I can own. Second, the macro changed underneath the whole theme — the 30-year cleared 5.1%, TLT is at a 22-year low, and utilities broke to 52-week lows while the index rose. Long-duration capex equities derate in that tape, so I trim the two fattest multiples I own (GEV at 44.7x after a profit miss, VRT at 33.5x) rather than defend them. Third, my mandate calls for a small laggard short that I have not been carrying, and the regime finally names it: I own the sellers of AI infrastructure, so I short CoreWeave, the buyer funding $35-39B of 2026 capex on $35B of debt while losing money. If AI financing strain is real my longs survive it and CRWV does not; if NVDA blows out on Aug 26 the short pays for itself out of my longs. I am at -14.61% drawdown, the exact tolerance this mandate was written to respect, so I take net exposure from 82% to 72% long against a 6% short and hold 22% cash at 4% instead of adding the 3x-semis kicker — that kicker is capped by the drawdown limit, and the drawdown limit is where we are.

    Two things changed this week and both point the same way. First, my own regime call from last week was confirmed rather than refuted: a solid payroll print (162k) on Sept 4 pushed yields and the dollar up, the Dow sank on rate fears, and inside that tape the market paid only for near-term cash earnings. MU (7.07x forward) rose 9.0% on the week to $1,016.59; AMAT fell 13.7% over the month, AVGO fell 14.9%, COHR 15.7%, FN 25.1%, and CRDO fell 26.7% in five sessions after BEATING on Q1 FY27 ($479M rev, $1.20 EPS) and guiding Q2 to $525-535M. Broadcom did the identical thing on Sept 2 - revenue $29.6B, up 86% year over year, guided $34.8B against $35.0B consensus, stock -6%. When a company grows 86% and the stock falls on a 0.6% guidance miss, the marginal buyer is not paying for the story any more, and my AMAT and AVGO legs are exactly that trade. They go. Second, the money that left is visibly arriving somewhere specific: Bridgewater more than doubled Vistra while cutting NVIDIA 18%, Thiel disclosed $59M in VST, VST's CEO bought $1.17M of stock after a 29% decline, Microsoft and Meta signed multi-decade nuclear supply deals, and CEG signed ~1GW of long-term nuclear contracts and raised FY26 EPS guidance to $11.50-12.50. The independent power complex rallied 7-9% on the week while sitting 25-35% below its 52-week highs and DOWN on the year (CEG -18.0%, VST -9.4%, TLN -20.1%). That is the rare combination my mandate is supposed to hunt: an unambiguous physical bottleneck in the buildout, a fresh dated catalyst, and an expectations reset that has already happened. So I am rotating the book one step further down the same axis I chose last week - from silicon toward electrons and bits - and I am cutting the two legs my own framework condemns, ANET at ~42x and GEV at ~42x forward, back to zero and 6 respectively even though ANET held up this week, because I will not keep 42x long-duration multiples in a book whose thesis is that the market has stopped paying for them. I am also closing the CoreWeave short. It is down 5.27% on the leg and the reason it existed is gone: CRWV printed $2.58B of Q2 revenue up 112%, Truist raised to $165, it rose 5.7% on Friday, and paying 3% borrow to be short the momentum leader in the sector my longs depend on is a hedge that fights my own book. I would rather hold 26% in cash at 4% than run a short I no longer believe. Net result: gross falls slightly to 74%, the short book goes to zero, and half of the remaining risk sits in near-term-cash-earnings power at 10-24x instead of story silicon at 25-42x.

    Registered book note — experiments/round2/weeks/2026-09-16/opus_picks_and_shovels.json

    The mandate is long the physical bottlenecks of the AI buildout AT THE CHEAP END OF THE MULTIPLE AXIS. Over the last six weeks that axis has split in two and I was on the wrong side of the split. The macro is the cause: the Saudi East-West pipeline was shut after drone attacks, crude is above $100 with roughly 4% of global supply at risk, and the resulting inflation impulse has pushed the 10-year briefly through 5% with TLT pinned at its 52-week low. Anything whose value is a long stream of future cash flows has been marked down mechanically. That is exactly what my electron sleeve is. XLU trades at $41.61 against a 52-week low of $41.52; TLN is at $286.56 against a 52-week low of $285.86 with negative GAAP EPS; CEG is $262 against a $412 high; VRT is $239 against $380 at 54x trailing; GEV is $883 at a 41.6x FORWARD multiple with a fresh sell initiation at $470. None of those are cheap. Holding them is not conviction, it is refusing to mark my own thesis to the tape - the book is -13.39% and this leg alone is -6% to -17% across every line. Meanwhile the other half of the mandate has been marked down just as hard but arrives cheap on the way out: SNDK at a 7.28x forward multiple on revenue +175%, WDC at 17.6x on net income +399% and 47% off its high, MU at 20.9x on revenue +167% and net income +711%, all after Monday's memory selloff on AI-capex-pause chatter that is already reversing. So I am not abandoning the strategy, I am enforcing the half of it I have been under-honoring. Two specific swaps carry the reasoning. First, STX out and WDC in: same physical bottleneck - nearline HDD for AI data lakes - at 17.6x instead of 57.9x, which is the multiple-axis discipline applied literally. Second, three electron legs down to one, keeping only VST, because it is the leg with real cash generation (Q2 adjusted EBITDA +30% YoY to $1.77B), insider buying, and genuine upside from a gas-price shock that widens spark spreads, rather than the leg with the best story. I am also raising cash from 26% to 32%: the FOMC decides on my entry date into an oil-driven inflation print, the resulting book is concentrated in a single volatile factor, and I would rather express that concentration in selection than in gross. Honest bear case, stated so it is on the record: a 7x forward multiple on a memory name is as often a peak-earnings signal as a bargain, and MU reports 9/30 inside the holding period. That is what the stops are for.

Take-profit set at 30% because a supply-disruption rally is by construction reversible the moment pumping resumes.

Where XLE dilutes crude beta through downstream, XOP is undiluted upstream: with the East-West pipeline offline and 4% of global supply in question, realised prices flow to these income statements almost immediately and equal weighting stops the exposure collapsing into two mega-caps. I size it below XLE and give it a tighter 16% stop precisely because that undiluted beta cuts both ways - this is the leg that round-trips fastest if Saudi pumping resumes within days, which is the explicit condition the reporting attaches to the whole shock.
EWZequitylong17.0%—−18%+35%Raised from 12 to 17 and now the largest non-energy leg, because it is the one equity market that sits on the winning side of every axis in this shock at once. Brazil trades at a 10.1x PE with a 3.59% dividend yield after a +31% year, it is a net energy exporter with Petrobras and a commodity exporter with Vale at 9.8% of the fund, and a Nu Holdings and Itau financial complex that benefits from high domestic real rates rather than being crushed by them. It is my best-performing leg at +4.94% and it has an October general election as a dated catalyst. This is where the money cut from Europe and Japan goes: same 'international value' exposure the mandate asks for, but on the exporter side of the terms-of-trade line instead of the importer side.
GDXequitylong15.0%—−15%+35%Held essentially flat at 15 as the deliberate hedge against the rest of this book rather than as an expression of it. Gold at $393.60 on GLD is 23% below its $509.70 high and is testing its 200-day with a near-5% ten-year as a live headwind, which is why this leg is -4.35%. I keep it because the FOMC decides on my entry date and the branch that hurts everything else I own is the branch this leg needs: a Fed that accommodates an oil-driven inflation impulse rather than fighting it debases the real return on every energy and EM dollar in the book, and $18B flowed into gold ETFs in August on precisely that sovereign-debt and debasement fear. Miners rather than bullion because their operating leverage means a modest gold move pays for a large equity drawdown elsewhere. Stop tightened to 15% given the yield headwind.
COPXequitylong12.0%—−16%noneCut from 15 to 12 rather than eliminated. The case against it is that it is the most demand-elastic commodity I own and my worst leg at -8.28%: $100 crude plus a 5% ten-year is a tax on global industrial activity, and copper feels a growth slowdown well before oil does, which is why it is 15% off its $99.99 high while energy sits at its highs. The case for keeping a tail is that copper's bid is increasingly structural rather than cyclical - grid and data-centre electrification from the AI buildout is a supply-constrained, multi-year demand source that does not care about one quarter of PMI - and the fund is still +63.6% over the year. Halving the cyclical risk while keeping the structural option is the right size for a leg I believe in over years and distrust over months; the 16% stop is tightened from 18% to enforce that distrust.

Cash to 7%; at a 4% APY there is no case for holding more when every real-asset leg just got a monetary tailwind.

  9. 2026-09-16REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-16/opus_picks_and_shovels.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-16/opus_picks_and_shovels.json

    This book is +13.59% and the thesis is being confirmed, so the temptation is to leave it alone. I am trading anyway, because a specific and dateable event has made half of it wrong even as the other half works. Saudi Arabia shut its East-West crude pipeline after drone attacks, roughly 4% of global supply is at risk unless pumping resumes within days, and crude is above $100 with USO at $158.90 against a 52-week high of $160.27 and a low of $65.99. That is not the gentle commodity reflation this basket was built for; it is a hard terms-of-trade shock, and a terms-of-trade shock sorts countries into winners and losers far more sharply than 'international value' does. My EZU and EWJ legs sit on the losing side of that sort and I put them there before the sort existed. The eurozone imports its energy and the ECB has just RAISED to 2.5% into what the tape is calling an energy-led inflation spike, with more tightening expected - that is an importer taking the price shock and the monetary response at the same time, and EZU is already my second-worst leg at -2.90%. Japan is the same trade in a different currency. Both are cut to zero. The proceeds go to the exporters and to the commodity itself. I split energy rather than simply doubling XLE, because XLE is 35% ExxonMobil and Chevron - integrateds whose downstream partly offsets a crude spike - while XOP is equal-weighted E&P at an 11.6x multiple versus XLE's 17.2x, which is where the crude beta actually lives. EWZ goes up because Brazil at 10.1x with a 3.6% yield is a commodity and net-energy exporter with an October election catalyst, and it is my best-performing leg at +4.94%. COPX is halved: copper is the most demand-cyclical thing I own, it is my worst leg at -8.28%, and $100 crude plus a 5% ten-year is a global growth tax that hits industrial demand before it hits oil. GDX is held nearly flat at 15 and I want the reasoning recorded because it looks inconsistent - gold is struggling at its 200-day with 5% yields as a direct headwind, and if the FOMC is hawkish tomorrow it gets worse. I hold it precisely because the FOMC is tomorrow and the other branch is live: a Fed that accommodates an oil-driven inflation shock rather than fighting it is the single scenario that hurts every other leg's real return, and $18B went into gold ETFs in August on exactly that fear. GDX is the hedge against my own book, not a momentum bet. Finally, the strategy of record mentions a small dollar short and I am continuing to omit it deliberately rather than by oversight: the US is a net energy exporter and the Fed is the least dovish central bank in this shock, so an oil spike is dollar-positive on both terms of trade and rate differential. Shorting the dollar here would be following the mandate's letter into a losing trade. Gross comes down from 84 to 80 into the FOMC; the sharpening is in composition, not in leverage.

WHERE MONEY IS GOING: healthcare is the decisive leader and it is broad, not one name — XLV +13.9% 3m/+23.9% 12m, VHT +14.3% 3m, LLY +29.5%, ABBV +24.6%, MRK +19.4%, JNJ +15.5%, UNH +13.5%, IBB +11.8%, PPH +11.4%, IHI +7.9% in 5d. XLV sits +6.8% over its 50d and +9.2% over its 200d. TWO KEY NEGATIVE FINDINGS THAT CHANGED MY BOOKS:
1) QUAL is the wrong quality vehicle. MSCI USA Quality is heavy in exactly the megacaps de-rating: -0.6% 1m versus XLV +3.4% and SCHD +6.0%. It delivered tech beta, not defense. 2) Gold is broken, and so are bonds. GLD -22.1% 6m, -4.1% below its 50d and -9.9% below its 200d; GDX -16.7% 3m, SLV -22.3%. The +2.7% gold pop on 7/29 is a bounce inside a confirmed downtrend. TLT is -5.3% 1m with 10y yields at 4.62% and rising. With both traditional hedges failing, cash at 4% APY is genuinely the superior non-equity ballast, so I zeroed the gold diversifier rather than keep hedging theater.

ON THE SMH SHORT (held in both books): the trend is my best idea, but SMH is now -15.5% below its 50-day while still +12.4% ABOVE its 200-day and +70% over 12 months. That is a violent correction inside a long-term uptrend, stretched and squeeze-prone. So I let it run at roughly existing size with stops attached, and deliberately did NOT add into the capitulation.

CRYPTO (Round 3): the trend filter says no. BTC -26.0% 12m, -10.1% 6m, -10.6% below its 200d. ETH -32.4% 12m, -11.7% 6m, -9.7% below its 200d — though ETH is +8.6% above its 50d and +10.0% 1m, the strongest short-term crypto momentum. Both majors below their 200-day means a trend-stacking mandate must cut, not hold. Also cut MTUM entirely (-15.7% 1m, -10.5% below its 50d) and cut JEPI hard — it is -2.9% over 6m, +0.1% over 12m and below its 200-day, i.e. dead money that only earns its keep as the option-carry mandate leg. Commodity/energy carry is the one genuinely confirmed, accelerating uptrend: PDBC +20.2% 6m/+30.2% 12m and +12.6% over its 200d, XLE +18.1% 6m/+33.8% 12m.

QUALequitylong9.0%—−12%noneBalance-sheet-quality factor exposure: high ROE, low leverage, stable earnings. In a higher-for-longer rate path the refinancing wall is the dominant equity risk and this screen is the cleanest way to own the companies that do not have one. Nudged from 8% to 9% because quality is the factor that should lead if the Fed hikes again, and it is the only factor sleeve here I want larger rather than smaller.

Cut from 11% to 8%: enough to keep the volatility dampener, small enough that it stops being the second-largest drag on a rising 10-year.
XLPequitylong5.0%—−10%noneA small new staples sleeve funded by the GLD exit. Staples have been the worst defensive sector of the last year (+7%) and that is precisely the argument for a 5% position: it is the one genuinely low-beta sector nobody is crowded into, and with CPI at 3.4% the pricing-power names carry cost inflation through rather than absorb it. Deliberately capped at 5% because the sector also carries the same duration problem as USMV; this is diversification of the defensive bucket, not a call.

    Stated reason (desk log)

    The tape is validating this mandate precisely — capital is rotating out of the AI-capex complex into cheap defensive cash-flow — so the fix is not to change the strategy but to stop diluting it. Three changes. (1) XLV 19% to 36%: healthcare is the single highest-conviction idea available to a defensive book right now, leading on 1m (+3.4%), 3m (+13.9%) and 12m (+23.9%), above both its 50- and 200-day, and broad across LLY/ABBV/MRK/JNJ/UNH/IBB rather than resting on one name. Free sizing exists for exactly this. (2) QUAL 18% to zero, replaced by SCHD 16%: QUAL is ~30% technology and returned -0.6% over the month while the defensives it was supposed to sit beside made money — it was selling me tech beta under a quality label. SCHD applies a return-on-capital and FCF/leverage screen without the AI-bubble exposure and beat it on every horizon (+15.2% 6m, +26.0% 12m). This keeps the quality-factor leg of the mandate and fixes the vehicle. (3) GLD 6% to zero and SPLV 11% folded into USMV. Gold is -22% over six months and below both moving averages; with TLT also -5.3% on the month, both traditional hedges have failed, and cash at 4% APY is the honest defensive ballast. SPLV and USMV are near-duplicate min-vol exposures, and SPLV's utilities tilt is a liability with yields rising (XLU -2.4% 1m), so I consolidated into the better-diversified one.     Weekly desk 2026-08-08: The July payroll print (-23,000 jobs) flipped the regime my 7/31 book was built for, and it did so in a way that hurts one leg and helps the mandate everywhere else. Two changes follow from that, and I am deliberately not touching the rest. First, the semis short: my thesis was 'AI-infra overextended,' the bust actually happened (-20% in a month), and it was bought back with both hands the moment the Fed turned dovish — SMH +7.80% in a week, +103% over twelve months, still 27.8% above its 200-day. Insurance that pays out against my longs falling is worth carrying; insurance whose losses are driven by the same rate-cut impulse that lifts my longs is not insurance at all, it is an uncorrelated short in the market's highest-beta index. I cut it in half and tighten the stop so a full stop-out from here costs 32bp instead of ~1%. This is also the complex where 5 of 17 standing orders died on 8/07 alone; I am sizing to survive a squeeze rather than to be right about it. Second, my mandate names a gold diversifier and my book has had none — an omission the tape just punished. Gold broke out on soft jobs, a weaker dollar, falling real yields and record PBoC buying; bullion is the low-volatility way to own that, unlike the miners which just went up 21% in five sessions. I fund it by trimming XLP, which is the only defensive sleeve failing to participate (+1.96% over three months). Crucially I am NOT retreating from the defensive stance: a shrinking labour market is precisely the environment where healthcare, quality cash-flow and min-vol earn their keep over the next several quarters, so XLV stays the conviction position at a third of the book.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: Two things forced my hand and I am changing nothing else. First, the semis short has failed the test I explicitly wrote down for it. Two weeks ago I halved it and said I would not call the view dead because SMH was 'still 4.6% below where it was a month ago and below its 50-day.' Both conditions have now flipped: SMH closed 594.07, up 4.3% on its month-ago level after running from the 569-575 shelf, and has reclaimed the 50-day. That is my own stated falsification condition triggering, so I close it. My valuation view is unchanged — 44x earnings and still 11.6% under the 671.83 six-month high — but I have been wrong on timing two weeks running, and paying 3% borrow to hold an opinion that keeps costing me is not discipline, it is stubbornness. I would rather re-enter on a failed rally than keep bleeding into a rate-cut bid. Second, the macro tape has resolved into a debasement signature: the dollar fell 1.7% on the month and made a fresh low, gold rose 12%, and the 10-year backed UP 19bp to 4.738% while the front end rose only 6bp. Rising long yields with a falling dollar is the one configuration that specifically punishes bond-proxy defensives and specifically rewards bullion. So gold goes from 8% to 11% — still 'small' as my mandate requires, and still a diversifier rather than a core — and staples, the leg that has now been flat for three consecutive assessments, funds part of it. The rest goes to SCHD, whose cash-flow-and-return-on-capital screen is the defensive expression that does not depend on falling long rates. XLV I deliberately do not add to despite it being the best thing I own: +14% in a month leaves it 1.1% from its 52-week high, and adding there is chasing.

    The regime changed on me this week and it changed against one specific part of my book. Going into the week the market was pricing Waller's disinflation comments; by Friday's close August payrolls printed 162k against a ~55k consensus with June and July revised up a combined 55k, the 2-year yield jumped 3.8bp to 4.37% (highest since January 2025), the 10-year hit 4.78%, and short-rate futures moved to roughly a 58-65% probability of a HIKE at the September 15-16 FOMC. A defensive book is not automatically safe in that world: the bond-proxy defensives are precisely the trade that loses when the front end reprices higher. My previous book carried roughly 29% in rate-sensitive sleeves (XLP staples, USMV min-vol which is heavy utilities/staples/REITs, and GLD which is short real rates). So I am cutting XLP entirely, trimming USMV from 17 to 11 and GLD from 7 to 6, and moving the released weight into things that are defensive for reasons other than duration: healthcare earnings resilience, quality free cash flow, and cash itself. Second observation: this economy is bifurcated, not uniformly weak. Lululemon fell 17% on cut guidance and dragged the whole athletic-apparel complex, while semis and memory were the strongest part of Friday's tape on continued AI demand. That says consumer-facing staples/discretionary is the wrong place to hide and that a modest allocation to broad quality (which now carries real megacap-tech cash-flow weight) is a better quality expression than more staples. Third, Brent is near $95 on US-Iran tension and refinery disruption, which is both an inflation risk to the Fed path and an earnings tailwind to integrated energy, so I am adding a small XLE sleeve as a hedge that actually earns something rather than adding more gold. Finally, with the Fed possibly hiking, 22% cash at 4% is a genuine competing asset, not a drag - I am willing to hold it and stay ahead of SPY on a risk-adjusted basis rather than reach. Book is up 3.18% vs SPY 2.59% with a 1.70% max drawdown; the job is to keep that profile intact through a hawkish FOMC, not to chase.

    The regime finally resolved and it resolved against my gold leg. Fed funds have sat at 3.75% since June, three members dissented in July for a hike, August CPI printed 3.40% y/y, and the 10-year is at its highest since 2007 with crude at $100 after a Saudi pipeline outage that threatens ~4% of global supply. In that setup gold is not an inflation hedge, it is an unlevered short-real-rate position: GLD is 23% below its 52-week high of 509.70 and my 6% leg is the worst performer in the book at -1.70%. I am cutting GLD to zero and moving the inflation-hedge role to energy, which does the same job with actual free cash flow, a 17x P/E, a 2.3% yield and a price near its 52-week high. XLE doubles from 6% to 12%. I also trim the two most rate-sensitive quality sleeves: USMV 11 to 8 and SCHD 17 to 15, because min-vol and high-dividend screens both drag in utilities and staples that de-rate as the long end rises. XLV stays the anchor at 29% because the rotation out of crowded semis is landing in healthcare and the sector is up ~5% since mid-July while SPY is flat. I hold cash at 22% rather than raising it: my fill is at the 2026-09-16 close, after the FOMC reaction is already in the price, so I am not paid to hide from the event itself. Total one-way turnover is roughly 12% of the book, about a quarter of a basis point in commissions, which is the right price for swapping a losing hedge for a working one.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: This is a trend-stacking mandate and the cross-asset trend set genuinely changed, so re-racking is the discipline, not churn. Three trends I owned rolled over and two I did not own turned up. The clearest signal of the week was not in my P&L, it was in oil: USO fell 8.66% in five sessions and 13.69% in two weeks, through its 50-day, while the headlines were as bullish as they get — Hormuz disruption, record refinery margins, supermajor profits surging on crude. A trend that cannot rally on its own best news is over, and a shrinking payroll count explains why. So XLE goes to zero and PDBC is cut from 24% to a residual. Second, I close the SMH short outright. Last week I wrote that I was applying the trend filter honestly; applying it honestly today means admitting that a name up 103% over twelve months, 27.8% above its 200-day, that just rose 7.8% in a week, is not a downtrend a trend book gets to be short. The intermediate dip was the countertrend, not the trend, and I was on the wrong side of my own rule. Third, the redeployment. EFA is the cleanest uptrend on my entire screen — positive on every horizon from one week to twelve months, above both moving averages — and a Fed cutting into a weak dollar is the structural tailwind for ex-US equity, so it becomes a core leg. IWM gets the equity-momentum slot: 13.3% above its 200-day and beating the S&P year-to-date, and small caps are the most direct expression of the rate-cut repricing. XLF adds trend plus dividend carry with far better credit quality than KRE, which I screened and rejected because regional-bank credit into a contracting labour market is the wrong risk to be paid for. JEPI is upgraded from a grudging stub to a real weight because it now clears the filter it failed on 7/31 — it has reclaimed its 200-day (+4.1%) and option-writing income is exactly the right carry to own if this melt-up turns choppy.     Weekly desk 2026-08-22: A trend mandate that cuts a leg for failing confirmation is obliged to add it back when confirmation arrives, otherwise the rule is not a rule. Last week I cut crypto to a 3% marker with a precise reason: ETH 'went nowhere in a week when every other asset class I track rallied — non-participation in broad risk-on is how a trend mandate identifies a dead trend.' That test has now been passed emphatically and in the cleanest possible shape. ETH sat between $1,860 and $1,915 for four straight weeks, then broke to $2,524 and settled at $2,427, +29%. BTC sat between $62.8k and $65.0k for three weeks, then went $64.7k, $69.4k, $73.1k, $78.3k and settled at $77,227, +20%. Long consolidation base, decisive break, shallow 1.4-4% pullback — that is the specific pattern this mandate exists to buy, and it is the strongest signal anywhere on my board. So crypto goes from a 3% marker to a 13% sleeve, and I add BTC alongside ETH because BTC is leading, is the lower-volatility expression, and diversifies the sleeve. I stay in spot rather than perps: the funding case has flipped in my favour now that the trend is up, but taking leverage into an asset that just moved 25% in four sessions is how you get liquidated on the retrace, and the 5%-of-margin liquidation threshold makes that a real risk rather than a theoretical one. Funding comes from the two weakest trends and from cash. IWM is the one leg that broke down rather than paused — it printed 305.18 and faded to 299.96 — and the rate move makes that worse, since the 10-year rose 19bp while the front end rose 6bp, which is the opposite of the cut-driven steepening that powered it. JEPI comes down two points because in a tape making new highs a written-call sleeve caps me by construction; the carry is still worth owning, just not at 15%. CPER gives back a point after fading 2.4% from its high. Everything else holds because it is working: DBMF and EFA are both within 1% of their highs, and EFA in particular is the direct mechanical beneficiary of a dollar that just made a fresh leg down.

JEPI up three, reversing last week's trim on the grounds I gave for it: I cut it because 'the tape is trending' and a covered-call sleeve is capped in a trending market. The tape stopped trending this week, and VIX near the bottom 2.3 percentile of its range going into payrolls, CPI and an FOMC with a coin-flip hike means I am buying a premium-harvesting sleeve when premium is cheap and the catalysts for it to fatten are on the calendar. XLF up two, on price rather than my old logic — I owe an honest correction there, in the leg thesis. The rest goes to cash at 4%, which in a hiking scare is a carry position that gets better if I am wrong about everything else. I am holding both crypto legs flat despite them being my strongest trend, because adding at the top of a 25% seven-session move is the same mistake I refused to make in gold miners; I let the stops carry the position instead and tighten ETH's, since a fixed dollar risk is a smaller percentage after the asset has appreciated.

    This book is my problem child and this week told me why. It is up 1.52% against SPY +3.62% and BTC +23.17% since inception, with a 4.44% max drawdown - so I have been paying the volatility of a trend book while collecting the return of a cash-plus book. The diagnosis is not that trend stopped working; it is that I was not actually in the trends. My mandate explicitly names equity momentum and I owned zero of it. My mandate names commodity carry and I ran it at 8% while Brent went to ~$95 on US-Iran tension and refinery disruption. My mandate names crypto trend and I ran BTC at 5% through a 23% move. Meanwhile my second- and third-largest sleeves were JEPI and EFA, neither of which is a trend expression at all. Friday's tape sharpened this: August payrolls printed 162k versus ~55k expected with upward revisions to June and July, the 2-year yield jumped to 4.37% - its highest since January 2025 - and hike odds for the September 15-16 FOMC moved to roughly 58-65%. Two direct consequences. First, EFA has to go: a hawkish repricing strengthens the dollar, and unhedged developed international is a levered short-dollar position I am not being paid to hold. Its 0.84% gain is a gift I should take before the currency leg turns. Second, higher-for-longer is genuinely good for the front-end-sensitive carry I do want - bank net interest margins and the short-rate leg inside managed futures - so XLF stays and DBMF stays large. On the trend side, semis and memory were the strongest complex on Friday against a consumer that is visibly cracking (Lululemon -17% on cut guidance, dragging the whole athletic complex), which is the cleanest momentum signal available; I am adding MTUM as the broad equity-momentum sleeve the mandate always called for and SMH as the concentrated expression of it. Commodity carry goes from 8% to 12% because $95 Brent with a live geopolitical bid is exactly the backwardated-carry environment PDBC is built for. Crypto goes from 13% to 16%, with the increase going entirely into BTC (5% to 8%) so the sleeve is now balanced 8/8 rather than tilted toward the leg that has lagged; BTC is the asset actually trending and it is the one I was most underweight. I keep 15% cash at 4% as dry powder into an FOMC that could go either way. This is deliberately a different book from my Round 2 defensive core - there is zero symbol overlap with it, by design.

    Last leg I said this book would own the three trends that were actually working: commodity/energy carry, AI-led equity momentum, and crypto trend. One week of honest marks says only one of those three is still true, so I am rebuilding around it instead of defending the other two. What worked: DBMF +3.08% and PDBC +3.58%, both now sitting at 52-week highs, with PDBC +56% over twelve months. What did not: SMH -4.58% and MTUM -2.56%. Semis are 19% below their 52-week high of 671.83 and the tape has flipped them from the consensus safe AI play into the market's pain trade on hyperscaler capex fears and Chinese catch-up; MTUM is not a diversifier from that, it IS that, with AMD, Micron and Intel as its top three holdings at nearly 15% combined. Crypto is not a trend either - BTC at 76,176 is down 2.5% today and roughly 46% over twelve months, with a Senate Clarity Act vote as an open regulatory overhang. A bounce off a low is not a trend and a trend-stacking book should not pretend otherwise, so BTC and ETH go to zero, which is the single largest change here at 16% of gross. The macro backdrop justifies leaning the other way: Fed funds 3.75% with three July dissents for a hike into a live 2026-09-16 meeting, August CPI 3.40%, the 10-year at its highest since 2007, and crude at $100 after a Saudi pipeline outage that threatens ~4% of global supply. That is a commodity-carry regime and a long-duration-equity headwind, so I stack DBMF and PDBC to 38% combined, add two new cash-yield carry sleeves in AMLP and XOP, and convert the semiconductor exposure from a 5% long into a 6% short. I hold 16% cash at 4% rather than fully deploying because the entry fill is at the 2026-09-16 close and I would rather have dry powder than leverage into the Fed. Gross falls from 85% to 84% but the composition is almost entirely new; realised turnover is the price of admitting two of three legs of the old thesis are dead.

    The inflation-shock regime this book was built to hedge has actually arrived, and that forces two changes. WTI is $103.50 and Brent $107.50 and still rising on a Saudi pipeline outage from drone strikes that takes weeks to repair, US diesel has hit a record $6/gal, refiner margins printed record highs, and Strait of Hormuz risk is live. That oil shock has pushed the 10-year Treasury yield briefly above 5% for the first time since 2023 while the Fed funds rate sits at 3.75% -- the market is now debating hikes, not cuts, into the 2026-09-16 FOMC. Change one: I am cutting ORCL (13%), HUBS (6%) and INTU (6%) outright. My mandate is to buy capitulated dislocations, but a dislocation is only a buy when the discount is sentiment rather than deterioration. ORCL is down ~57% from $329.50 to $141.20 because it is funding an enormous AI capex build with debt; a 10-year above 5% makes that funding cost genuinely worse, so the bear case is strengthening with the tape, not fading. HUBS (+4.74%) and INTU (+5.31%) are long-duration multiples I am happy to ring the register on before a hawkish Fed repricing rather than after. Change two: I am raising energy from 11% to 21% via XOM and CVX. Note I deliberately did NOT chase VLO despite a 7.9x forward PE -- it has run from $155 to $391 on crack spreads at record highs, and buying record margins at 52-week highs is the opposite of a mean-reversion mandate. Cheap integrateds are the mandate-consistent expression. ADBE replaces ORCL as the software dislocation because it is the same setup without the balance sheet: it beat and raised FY26 on Sep 10 and still sold off on a soft Q4 guide, at 9.9x forward earnings, asset-light and cash-generative instead of levered into a capex race. Cash stays at 20% -- with the S&P at 25.8x and the long bond at 5%, the equity risk premium is roughly zero and 4% risk-free is a real competitor for capital, not a placeholder.

JNJequitylong6.0%—−10%noneThe 63-year dividend king and one of two remaining AAA-rated corporate balance sheets in the United States.
