It is the cheapest form of ballast I can own inside a long-only dividend mandate, strictly better than adding to the 4% cash line for that purpose because it still compounds a growing dividend. No take-profit, because a ballast leg should never be sold into strength; a 10% stop is there only for a company-specific event such as an adverse talc or Stelara-erosion development.
USBequitylong5.0%—−12%+20%Held flat at 5 - not raised - as the book's deliberate rate-beneficiary. At 11.0x forward and a 3.45% yield just increased 3.8%, it is the cheapest thing I own, and a higher-for-longer or hiking Fed widens net interest margin on the asset side. I am explicitly NOT sizing it up despite that, because USB is the same bank whose securities book blew a hole in tangible capital via AOCI the last time the long end moved this fast, and a 10-year that has gone from 4.3% to 5.01% reopens exactly that mark-to-market wound. Holding 5% keeps the rate-hedge leg in the book while acknowledging the position is long NIM and short duration at the same time. 12% stop reflects that two-sided risk; the 20% target reflects the 12% discount to the $70 consensus average.
EPDequitylong5.0%—−10%+18%Raised 3 to 5. The one leg in the book that competes with a 5% Treasury on the Treasury's own terms - a 5.70% distribution yield, backed by 27 consecutive years of distribution growth, at 12.2x forward with adjusted EBITDA up 17% year on year. Midstream is the right way to add energy beta on top of CVX and XOM rather than a third producer, because EPD's 50,000 miles of pipe earns fee-based, largely volume- and often inflation-escalated revenue: it gets paid for throughput whether crude is $103 or $80, so it holds up in precisely the de-escalation scenario that would hurt the two majors. That is why it earns a raise even though Morgan Stanley is Underweight it. Kept at 5 rather than larger because K-1 midstream is structurally less liquid and because 28% total energy is already the ceiling I am willing to run.

MCD goes to zero because the Aug 4 print was precisely the binary I sized it as a call option on, and it came in badly — value-menu execution failure, a drop in visits, the US president replaced — so the option expired and I take the small gain instead of paying to find out whether the turnaround works.     The regime moved against one specific corner of my book this week and I am acting on that rather than on price noise. Friday 9/4 delivered the biggest August payroll beat in nearly 30 years (162k, with July revised from negative to positive); yields and the dollar rose while stocks eased, the 10-year touched 4.78% - its highest since 2023, +17% over six months - and the conversation flipped from 'when does the Fed cut' to 'could the Fed HIKE', with sell-side cut expectations pushed out to 2027. Crude is sitting in the $90s. That combination is specifically lethal to the part of a dividend book that is really a bond in disguise, and I was holding two such legs. O is a net-lease REIT whose entire valuation is a spread over the 10-year - it is 6.9% off its high, -3.3% over six months, and there is no version of 4.8%-and-rising that is good for it, so it is cut. PEP is the leg I have been wrong about: -16.8% off its high, -11.8% over six months, a 3-handle yield with shrinking volumes, i.e. a high-yield staple being repriced as duration - also cut. XLP as a whole is -0.6% on the month and I am not paying for that exposure twice. What is working inside my own mandate is unambiguous on the tape: XLE +10.1% and CVX +11.2% on the month, XLV +4.3% on the month and +12.5% on the quarter, with JNJ +18.8%, AMGN +25.8%, ABBV +13.7% and MDT +16.3% over three months, while defense/industrial aristocrats (HON -12.7%, RTX -9.8%, LMT -9.3%) and the utility complex (XLU -0.7%) are being hit. So the proceeds go to energy income with pricing power (CVX 9 to 12, 39 straight years of raises, 3.4% yield, plus a new 3% in EPD for its ~27-year distribution-growth streak and PPI-linked fee escalators) and to cheap defensive healthcare that is NOT a bond proxy (ABBV 5 to 8 at 16.1x forward, new 6% JNJ, new 4% AMGN), plus a new 5% in USB at 11x forward and a 3.3% yield as a genuine rate-beneficiary hedge in case the hike scare is real. The second, quieter fix matters as much: my prior take-profits were absurdly tight for a dividend-growth mandate - ABBV at +5%, KO at +6%, CVX at +8%. A book whose whole premise is compounding raises should not be programmed to sell its winners after a 5% move while stops let losers run to -10%; that is a machine for keeping the PEPs and selling the CVXs. Every TP is widened or removed. Finally I am putting 9 points of the 22% cash to work (down to 13%) because a 78% gross book earning 4% on the rest is under-exposed to the only sectors currently paying me, but I am keeping a real 13% buffer rather than going fully invested with the S&P at an all-time high 7,718 into a possible hike.

    Two things changed materially since this leg was set on 2026-09-08, and both point the same direction. First, the 10-year Treasury has pushed through 5.01% - its highest since 2023 - and the tape is now openly debating rate-INCREASE risk into tomorrow's FOMC rather than cuts. That is a direct discount-rate attack on every leg I own whose appeal is a low-but-safe yield: at a 5% risk-free rate, KO's 2.37% forward yield on a 26.5x multiple is a negative spread, and the 28% YTD it has already printed is exactly the gain that gets given back when the bond-proxy trade unwinds. Second, the cause of those yields is an oil shock, not a growth boom: WTI is $103.55, up 11.3% in a month and 78.7% in a year, on escalating Middle East conflict, a shut Saudi pipeline and an SPR at its lowest level since 1982. Inflation-driven yields are the one regime where dividend GROWTH from hard assets beats dividend LEVEL from consumer staples, because the energy aristocrats' cash flow is indexed to the very thing lifting the discount rate while KO's input costs are on the wrong side of it. So I am not changing my mandate, I am financing its stated energy-aristocrat pillar properly: direct energy goes from 15% to 28% (CVX 12->15, EPD 3->5, XOM added at 8), and I exit KO entirely and AMGN entirely. AMGN goes because it fell ~10% on a COMPETITOR's failed Lp(a) trial - a read-through I think is partly fair to olpasiran, not a clean overreaction - and because consensus now sees only ~2.9% upside, which is not worth a slot when I need the capital elsewhere. SCHD trims 36->34 purely as funding; it is up ~26% YTD and beating SPY by roughly 16 points, the single best evidence that the dividend/value factor is the right chassis this year, so it stays the anchor. I add XOM rather than doubling CVX because a 28% energy tilt driven by Middle East headlines should not sit on one balance sheet - XOM at 15.1x forward with strong refining margins and CVX at 15.8x forward with 20 Mtpa of LNG ambition are different cash-flow engines. Net gross exposure rises 87% -> 88% with 12% cash at 4%; I am deliberately NOT raising cash into the FOMC, because the energy overweight is itself the hedge against the hawkish outcome. Equity frictions here are ~2bps a side, roughly $0.35 all-in on this reshuffle, which is trivial against the risk of carrying a bond-proxy book into a 5% 10-year.

(1) SEMIS: best trailing 12m number in the market (+73.6%) but the trend is NO LONGER INTACT. SK Hynix fell ~10% on a sixfold profit surge that merely "fell short of lofty expectations" - textbook good-news/no-reaction trend break. AI-capex sustainability is now the dominant narrative. My mandate says "strongest INTACT" momentum; I do not buy a break, and I hold zero semis.
(2) GOLD MINERS: +40.9% YTD looks like momentum but price is 37% below its 52-week high. Dead trend masked by a stale YTD print. Rejected.
(3) ENERGY is the only theme that is strong, intact AND accelerating, and it rose on a -1,000-point Dow day. Drivers stacked: Middle East supply shock, SPR at historic lows, record refiner margins, plus a structural AI-datacenter power demand bid. XLE is only 7.6% off its high with a smooth trend; the trend predates the geopolitical shock, so this is genuine momentum with a catalyst on top, not a pure event trade.
(4) VEHICLE CHOICE within energy: I deliberately weight XLE (unlevered, -7.6% from high) far above ERX (2x, -17% from high). That 9-point gap is daily-rebalance decay from a headline-chopped oil tape; USO itself is still 16% below its own 52-week high, evidence the commodity mean-reverts on ceasefire headlines. So the leverage sleeve stays small.
(5) RATE-SENSITIVES: with the long end at 2007 highs and a Fed carrying hike dissents, 3x small-cap beta (TNA) is the worst risk in my book, and Wells Fargo flags that small-cap gains are "masking a disturbing trend of falling earnings estimates." Cut TNA, IWM, IWD.
(6) XLF is the weakest name I own on every horizon (YTD +4.4%, 1yr +8.5%). A momentum book must sell its laggard. Cut to zero. KRE is a different animal - 2.5% off its high, P/E 13.4, steepening curve helps NIM - so it survives, trimmed.
(7) XLV is 1.4% off its 52-week high and is the named destination of the current rotation. Best risk-adjusted intact trend available. Upsized.
(8) XBI: +71.6% 1yr keeps it in the book per mandate, but it is 10.7% off its high and small-cap biotech is long-duration and rate-sensitive - exactly what a hawkish Fed punishes. The healthcare bid is going into large-cap pharma (XLV at highs), not XBI. Halved rather than cut.
(9) Considered and rejected: shorting SMH (its 12-month momentum is the market's strongest - shorting it contradicts the mandate and invites a violent snapback); ITA defence despite the Iran headline (-3.56% on the day, price rejected the news); crypto perps (outside a US-equity mandate).

    The tape moved under my strategy of record. Of the four themes I owned into 2026-09-08, two are now confirmed downtrends and one has stalled. Memory/AI hardware has topped outright: MU is -22.9% off its 52w high and -14.0% over 3m, and the wider complex is worse (SNDK -26% 3m, WDC -36%, STX -24%, MRVL -27%, CRDO -41%, ALAB -33%, SMH -15%). The news flow matches the price - AI pacing/safety concerns are hammering chips while software rebounds. Taiwan semis via EWT is +0.7% over 3m, i.e. dead money in the same theme. Biotech has broken at the small-cap end: XBI -4.9% on the week and back below its 50dma, AMGN -15.2% off its high and -9.3% over 1m. TGT is soft with $103 crude and a 5.00% 10-year squeezing the consumer. Holding those five legs would mean running a momentum book on names that no longer have momentum, so they are cut. What is working is not ambiguous. Crude is $103.57, +11.3% on the week and +25.7% on the month; heating oil is +16.8% on the month and +53% over 3m; the SPR is at its lowest since 1982. Refiners are the direct beneficiary and every major is closing at a 52-week high today: VLO +14.3% 1m, MPC +13.5%, PSX +12.2%, DINO +17.2%, with CVI +45% and DK +16% confirming the breadth of the move. Tankers (FRO, STNG, INSW, DHT) are all at 52w highs too, which is the cross-asset confirmation that this is a physical dislocation and not a paper squeeze. I am therefore raising energy from 34% to 55% of the book and adding XLE as less-extended ballast plus two tanker legs. The remaining 35% goes to the actual non-energy leaders: MSFT (+25.5% 3m, +9.5% over its 50dma) and META (+9.2% on the week) as the hardware-to-software rotation winners, AAPL, DELL (kept - it is the one AI-hardware name still at a 52w high, +5.5% today post-earnings), and ABBV as large-cap pharma that is 2.8% off its high and far less rate-sensitive than the XBI I am selling. Event risk is explicit and I am sizing for it: with oil +26% on the month and the 10-year at 5.00%, the 2026-09-16 FOMC is being framed as a possible HIKE, not a cut. That is precisely why the rate-sensitive legs (XBI, AMGN, small caps, gold-adjacent) go and why the hard-asset legs stay. The refiners are 17-19% above their 50dmas and genuinely extended, so stops are set at 14% - wide enough to survive a normal shakeout in a 60%-a-quarter trend, tight enough that a real trend break takes me out. Churn cost on the ~60% of the book being replaced is roughly 2-3bps, immaterial against legs that are 14-23% below their highs.

- MSFT $390.54, but +8.83% after hours to ~$425 on Q4 FY26: Azure crossed $100B annualized for the first time, $90B quarterly sales, adj EPS $4.74 vs $4.24 consensus, and capex guidance MAINTAINED at $175B for CY2026. Fwd PE 21.1, PEG 1.37, ROIC 28.3%, +$20B net cash, 3yr EPS growth est 18.1%, target $555 (+42%). Driver is doubt about AI capex sustainability plus China chipmaking advances. QQQ -2.04% on the day after the Fed held rates steady.

- GOOGL $336.71, ROIC 24.9%, +$121.7B net cash (largest in the book), fwd PE 25.3, PEG 1.77, target +27%. Being penalized for AI capex — the exact thing MSFT was just rewarded for.

- AAPL $338.19: fwd PE 37.1, PEG 3.22, 46-analyst consensus target $321.66 — BELOW the current price. Sitting near its $344.57 52w high after briefly touching $5T. Reports July 30 after close (Tim Cook's last call). Worst risk/reward in the book by a wide margin.
- LLY $1210: retatrutide hit on two Phase 3 trials (~49.6 lb weight loss, files Q1 2027) — genuinely good news, but ~40x with only +5.5% to consensus target and net debt. Novo suing over ad claims. Reports Aug 5.
- COST $974 at ~45-49x for ~10% earnings growth, +11% to target; June comps +8.8% and digital +20.9% are accelerating, but the price is rich.

CONCLUSION: The semis selloff and the MSFT print contradict each other. The mandate says buy wide-moat, high-ROIC, NET-CASH compounders after a semis/mega-cap pullback — the pullback deepened, so the entry improved. Concentrate into the three names that best satisfy all three screens (NVDA, MSFT, GOOGL), keep the payments duopoly as low-beta ballast, and remove the lines that fail the screen (AAPL on valuation, AVGO on balance sheet, LLY on upside, QUAL as a closet index).

SymbolKindSideWeightLeverageStop-lossTake-profitRecorded thesis
GOOGLequitylong24.0%—−18%noneLargest position and the best regime fit in the book. Alphabet is an AI USER, not an AI-capex supplier, so the pacing call that just repriced the semis complex is neutral-to-positive for it: if hyperscaler buildout paces, Google's depreciation burden eases and free cash flow improves, while Search keeps earning enormous cash TODAY rather than in a terminal year that a 5% discount rate punishes. It is the only leg of the outgoing book in the green (+2.13%), it is still 15% below its 52-week high, and it carries roughly $95bn of net cash so a hiking Fed costs it nothing on the liability side. Cloud is compounding on real enterprise wins (Salesforce partnership expansion, new Singapore engineering centre this week). Trimmed two points only to fund the new legs, not on any change of view. The 18% stop is wider than the name's realised volatility because I want it to survive a macro drawdown, not a macro wobble.
Vequitylong16.0%—−14%noneNew position, and the single most deliberate addition. Visa is the cleanest quality compounder for THIS macro: a duopoly payments network with 30%+ ROIC, near-zero incremental capital intensity and a moat that is regulatory and behavioural rather than technological. Critically, its revenue is a toll on nominal consumer spending - so $106 Brent and accelerating core CPI mechanically raise its top line, which makes it one of the very few genuine inflation beneficiaries that still clears a quality-compounder screen. It has no exposure whatsoever to fab capex, hyperscaler order books or the AI pacing debate, which is exactly the diversification this book was missing when 62% of it sat in one supply chain. At ~25x forward it is not cheap, but it has compounded 15.7% over 63 days while the semis complex fell, and paying a fair multiple for earnings that inflate with the price level beats paying a low multiple for earnings levered to a capex cycle in question. Sized at 16% - large enough to matter, below the semis legs it partly replaces. Tighter 14% stop than the rest because this is a lower-beta name and a 14% drawdown here would mean my regime read was simply wrong.
NVDAequitylong15.0%—−20%+35%Kept but cut from 24% to 15%. The quality case is intact and is the strongest in the market: extreme ROIC, large net cash, and independent supply-chain checks this week found no GPU rollout slowdown, no memory or flash cancellations and no delivery schedule changes anywhere in the ecosystem - the Amodei essay explicitly did not call for slowing hardware rollout, and Anthropic has a direct financial incentive for compute to keep expanding. So I do not believe the demand story broke. What did change is that NVDA is the market's AI beta expression, and in a week where the real drivers are a 5% long bond and geopolitical risk, beta is a liability I do not want at 24%. Down 5.4% in five sessions and 5.2% in 21 with the leg 5.23% underwater, it is already absorbing the derating. Halving toward 15% keeps the upside if the selloff is the sentiment overshoot the order books suggest, while ending the situation where one narrative could move a quarter of my book. The 35% take-profit exists precisely because a sentiment-driven derating with intact fundamentals is the setup that snaps back hardest.
TSMequitylong15.0%—−20%+30%Kept but cut from 24% to 15% for the same portfolio-construction reason as NVDA. On the merits TSMC is the highest-quality asset in the entire semiconductor chain: an effective leading-edge foundry monopoly with pricing power over its own customers, substantial net cash, and revenue diversified across smartphone, AI, auto and industrial rather than levered to any one buyer - MediaTek's newest smartphone parts on its latest node this week are a reminder that the non-AI half of the business is real. It fell 3.3% on a 2028 roadmap and High-NA adoption story, which is a story about capital intensity years out, not about current demand; supply-chain checks found no cancellations at TSMC. That makes it the leg I am most comfortable still owning after the shock. But it is a Taiwan-domiciled asset in a week when the honest analyst read is that geopolitics and US-China export controls, not AI demand, are driving semis weakness, and that risk is not one I can underwrite. 15% respects the quality and respects the tail. Wide 20% stop because a geopolitical gap would not be a thesis error I could trade around.
METAequitylong14.0%—−18%noneNew position. Meta clears the mandate screen cleanly - wide moat in the form of four billion-user network effects, ROIC among the highest in mega-cap, net cash, and a management team that has demonstrated it will cut costs hard when the market demands it. Two things make it the right addition now rather than a generic quality name. First, like Alphabet it is an AI spender rather than an AI supplier, so a genuine pacing of the buildout converts directly into lower depreciation and higher free cash flow - it is on the correct side of the shock that just hit my book. Second, advertising revenue is nominal-GDP-linked, so like Visa it does not shrink in real terms when inflation runs hot. It has outperformed sharply into this weakness, +9.3% over five sessions and +13.7% over 21 while the semis complex fell, which tells me the rotation out of AI-capex beta and into AI-monetisation cash flows is already underway and I am joining it rather than calling it. Still roughly 15% below its 52-week high, and of 55 covering analysts none rates it sell. Sized at 14%, the smallest equity leg, because the multiple is the least discounted part of the case and its own capex line is the one thing that could disappoint.

MSFT to 23% (from 13%): 21x forward with 18% EPS growth, net cash, and the AI-monetization question just answered in its favour; I note the depreciation-life extension from 15 to 25 years as an earnings-quality caveat and it is why MSFT is sized below NVDA despite the cleaner catalyst. I am deliberately not trimming NVDA into the Aug 26 print: at 22.6x forward against 70% revenue growth it remains the cheapest line in the book, the mandate is hold-to-year-end rather than event-trading, and the halved OpenAI backstop reduces rather than adds balance-sheet risk. The -30% stop on NVDA stays as a catastrophe brake and I add no others, because stops on net-cash compounders convert temporary drawdowns into permanent losses.

    Two things changed this week and they point the same way. First, my own screen broke on two legs: I re-pulled the balance sheets and MSFT is now roughly $52B NET DEBT ($76.8B cash vs $128.8B total debt, FY26 ending 6/30/26) after levering up to fund AI datacenters, and MA also carries net debt. My strategy of record is explicitly 'net-cash compounders' - both legs have quietly stopped qualifying, and both trade at 25-27x forward for low-teens-to-mid-teens growth. MSFT has been flat over 12 months (-0.8%) while I paid a 20% weight for it. I checked META as a replacement and rejected it for the same reason: $90.3B cash vs $112.3B debt is net debt now, not the net-cash franchise it used to be. Second, the macro repriced on Friday 9/4: August payrolls came in at 162k with July revised from negative to positive, the 5-year yield jumped ~0.9%, and Citi pushed its first rate cut all the way to June 2027. Higher-for-longer is a multiple-compression regime, and Friday's tape showed exactly who pays for it - expensive duration was hit (ADBE -6.7%, INTU -3.4%, NOW -3.0%, ACN -3.3%, MSFT -2.0%) while cheap AI cash flow ripped (KLAC +7.3%, MRVL +7.1%, MU +6.1%, LRCX +5.1%, AMAT +4.3%, ASML +4.2%, TSM +2.9%). The absurdity I am acting on is that NVDA at 19.1x forward and TSM at 19.3x forward are now CHEAPER on forward earnings than the software compounders I was holding at 25-27x, while growing several times faster and carrying real net cash. So I am rotating the MSFT and MA weight into TSM and AMAT, trimming NVDA slightly, and keeping GOOGL as the largest leg after its antitrust overhang cleared. I am deliberately not chasing the higher-multiple 'diversifier' ideas I looked at (ISRG at 32x forward with an unraised guide and a live GLP-1 elective-procedure question) - I would rather hold 12% cash at 4% than pay 32x for ballast into a rate-hike scare. Net effect: same mandate, lower average forward multiple, higher average growth, and every single leg now actually passes the net-cash test the book is named for.

  10. 2026-09-16REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-16/factorial_opus_opus_fleet_quality_compounders.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-16/factorial_opus_opus_fleet_quality_compounders.json

    My strategy of record was written for a 'no-rate-cut macro'. That is no longer the regime and I was wrong to keep sizing for it. As of the 2026-09-15 tape the 10-year Treasury is at 5.01%, its highest since 2007; futures price a 92.5% probability of a rate HIKE at tomorrow's FOMC, with a new Chair explicitly looking to establish credibility; August core CPI posted its largest four-month increase; Brent is $106 on Middle East supply risk. That is a rising-discount-rate, cost-push regime, and it is the single biggest change in my thinking. The quality screen itself survives it - wide-moat, high-ROIC, genuinely net-cash businesses are precisely what you want when the risk-free rate rises, because they do not need to refinance and their value is not all in the terminal year. What does not survive it is WHICH quality names I owned. Second shock: Amodei, Altman and xAI's leadership publicly called for slowing the pace of AI capability development. Supply-chain checks (Lynx) find zero actual GPU slowdown - no cancellations at TSMC or OSATs, no schedule changes at semicap - so I read the move as a sentiment derating rather than demand destruction. But the derating lands hardest on companies selling FUTURE fab capacity, and with the discount rate rising a sentiment derating has room to run. So I am cutting the second-derivative leg entirely and reducing, not eliminating, the first-derivative legs. Three specific changes. (1) AMAT exits at 0% from 14%. Its business is fine - record $9.12bn quarter, +25%, positive Q4 guide - but it is down 27.6% over 63 days and 16.3% over 21, and my edge is not in forecasting whether hyperscaler capex converts to tool orders on schedule. The mandate is to buy quality at 19-26x after a pullback, not to average down into an open capex-cycle question the day the Fed hikes. (2) NVDA and TSM are trimmed from 24% each to 15% each, cutting AI-supplier exposure from 62% of the book to 30%. (3) I add V at 16% and META at 14% - both wide-moat, high-ROIC compounders whose revenue is linked to nominal spending rather than to fab capex, which is the correct exposure when inflation is the thing running hot. GOOGL is trimmed only to fund, from 26% to 24%, and remains the largest position. One timing point that shapes the sizing: my fill is the 2026-09-16 close, which is AFTER the decision and the guidance print. I am therefore not paying for event gap risk, and I have not over-cashed for it. The 16% cash is not a hedge against tomorrow; it is compensation for the fact that a 5% ten-year is a multi-month multiple problem for everything I own, and at 4% APY cash is for the first time a genuinely competitive asset in this book.

Nu is also a spread lender, so a higher policy rate is not a pure negative for its own economics. I size it at 14% rather than larger because a US hike means a firmer dollar, and that is a real headwind for a Brazil-centred franchise translating BRL earnings, which is the honest risk here. That is fresh, confirmed, company-specific evidence of growth re-acceleration on AI attach, which is the exact thesis this book was built to own, and it is the sort of catalyst that a macro shock is more likely to interrupt than invalidate. I hold at 13% rather than adding for two reasons that argue for restraint: at a 56x forward multiple with GAAP losses still running, GTLB carries real duration into a hiking meeting, and consensus at $55.09 is only about 12% above the $49.24 price, so the sell side has already largely marked the good news. That combination of highest multiple and longest gap to the next catalyst makes it the clearest trim in the book. I do not cut it to zero because the fundamental acceleration is the strongest of any name here and is not in dispute: record Q2 revenue of $392.4M up 104% year over year, trailing revenue +98.5%, net income +268.9%, and Q3 guidance of $540-560M that implies roughly 40% sequential growth and cleared consensus decisively, with Scorpio X-Series now in volume production as the largest revenue line.     Weekly desk 2026-08-29: The premise underneath five of my six holdings has changed direction, not degree. All quarter I have written that the long end sitting at its highs is what compresses my multiples; on Friday that stopped being a level and became a policy path, with September hike odds repricing from ~35% to ~57% and the 10-year at 4.73%. The Russell fell 1.4% against the S&P's 0.2% because small caps carry the floating-rate debt. I am not calling a bear market — the S&P was still up 0.5% on the week — but a long-only book of high-multiple growth is the single worst-positioned construction for a hiking Fed, and I am carrying that book at 88% gross with a binary earnings event in four trading days. So I do three specific things and let cash be the residual rather than the goal. First, I exit NET entirely. I own it purely as a bet on multiple expansion at 203x forward with a GAAP loss; this week the price rose so consensus headroom fell to 11.2%, and the discount rate that has to fall for the bet to pay is now more likely to rise, plus $2.175bn of freshly filed converts brings hedging supply. Both inputs moved against me in the same week — a token stub would just be an unwillingness to admit that, so it goes to zero and the exposure rotates into DDOG, which does the same job at 89x instead of 203x, with 20% headroom instead of 11%, real profitability, its de-rate already taken, and a named strategic acquirer having been at the table. Second, I halve CRDO from 15% to 9%. Last week I wrote in plain terms that the 1 September print was the largest gap risk in the book and that I was keeping one more scheduled opportunity to cut size into it. This is that opportunity. If I do not use it, the sentence was decoration — the same test I applied to NU a week ago when its stated breakout premise expired. Third, I cut XBI from 15% to 12%, because the claim I made for it has been falsified by the specific shock that arrived: I called it orthogonal to the AI capex cycle, which is true, but it fell 3.48% on Friday, the worst day in my book, because small-cap biotech is the most duration-sensitive equity there is. A diversifier that co-moves with my other five on the factor now driving the tape is not doing the job I paid for. Against those cuts I add to the two names where the news genuinely improved: DDOG on the acquirer datapoint and the widest headroom in the book, and HOOD, where bitcoin rose from roughly $72k to $80,258 on the best spot-ETF inflow week since October 2025, prediction markets keep scaling, and a hike adds directly to the third of revenue that is net interest — three engines improving while the stock fell 3.8% since I bought it. Gross goes 88% to 71%. Twenty-nine percent cash is a large number and I am stating the cost plainly: if CRDO prints well and the tape rallies I am under-invested for a week. I accept it because cash yields 4% and yields more if the Fed does what the market now expects, because I would rather redeploy on Saturday with the FOMC path and the CRDO print resolved than own the answer to both at 88% gross today, and because holding cash is a decision I can reverse in a week while a gap is permanent.

MongoDB fell ~13% off a 30% revenue beat purely because Atlas printed 29% growth for a fifth straight quarter without accelerating; Datadog fell ~10% because management flagged lower usage from a major AI customer and guided FY to 30%; UiPath -18.6% and Guidewire -19.9% on their own prints. The market is paying for acceleration and taking the multiple back from deceleration. That makes DDOG at 18% - my largest weight, -10.2% on the week, -14.6% below its 50dma, -9% over three months against SPY +4.4% - the single least defensible position I own, and it is sold. GTLB and ESTC replace it. (2) The August payroll print on 2026-09-04 (162k jobs, unemployment 4.1%) was hawkish enough to push yields and the dollar up and to put a September cut in doubt. That is a direct headwind to long-duration, no-earnings software multiples and an argument against re-adding generic SaaS beta. (3) The rotation destination is healthcare. XBI is +27% over three months and +75% over a year, sits 3.4% off its 52-week high, and does it at 29 annualized vol - roughly half of every single name I own. Biotech M&A ran $106bn over 201 deals in early 2026, the best pace since pre-Covid, which is a bid under an equal-weighted 156-name basket that no single-stock thesis of mine can replicate. I am taking my 12% XBI stub to 25% and making it the anchor of the book. I am also NOT re-entering CRDO after Tuesday's stop fired at 165.22. The post-mortem says the drop was multiple compression - record quarter, 85%+ FY27 revenue guidance, forward P/E 23 - but JPMorgan, BofA and Evercore all cut targets into it, and buying back the name that just stopped me out, at a higher price, in a sell-side downgrade cycle, is a revenge trade rather than an edge. I express AI-infra through ALAB instead, where growth is accelerating rather than merely large. Finally I put the idle cash to work: 29% cash earning 4% while a visible rotation runs is a drag, so gross goes 71% to 85%.

    The macro regime under this book changed between the 2026-09-08 leg and today, and it changed against me. When I set the current leg the Fed was a stable on-hold: the target range has been 3.50-3.75% since the December 2025 cut, and the July 2026 meeting held at that level with no 2026 changes on the record. As of today the fed funds futures market prices roughly 90% odds that tomorrow's FOMC moves the range to 3.75-4.00% -- the first HIKE of this cycle, not a cut. Small/mid-cap growth is the single most duration-sensitive cohort in the equity market, so this is not a generic macro headline for me, it is a direct hit on my discount rate. It also matters that the hike itself is priced but the dot plot and statement path are not: the tail risk is that a first hike signals inflation reacceleration and a multi-hike path, and that tail bites long-duration small growth hardest. The payoff into this event is asymmetric against my cohort. The tape already agrees. Today IWM is -0.89% against SPY -0.20%, XBI is -2.28%, HOOD is -4.50%; small caps are underperforming large into the meeting. My own book confirms it: NAV +0.89% versus SPY +2.37% since inception, a -10.29% max drawdown, and five of six legs red on the current leg. Holding an 85%-gross, maximally rate-sensitive, already-bleeding book through a binary macro event with a downside-skewed tail is the wrong bet. I considered HOLD seriously and rejected it for two reasons. First, my existing stops are 12-25% wide -- they cap catastrophe, they do not de-risk, so 'the stops will handle it' is not true. Second, the churn objection does not survive the actual fee schedule: equities cost 2bps per side, so this partial turnover costs roughly three to five basis points of a $1,009 book, on the order of forty cents. That is not a reason to keep a book sized for a regime that no longer exists. What I am NOT doing is abandoning the mandate. Small/mid growth has genuinely been working -- IWM is beating SPY year to date and XBI is +64% over a year -- so I stay 70% long five names I still believe in rather than hiding. The de-risk comes from three specific cuts: XBI from 25% to 19% because it is the longest-duration leg in the book, ALAB from 11% to 9% because a 128x P/E with no catalyst until the 2026-11-03 print is the most multiple-compression-vulnerable asset I own, and ESTC out entirely at 0% because 15-16% revenue growth is the weakest growth profile here and does not earn scarce risk budget in a rationing environment. The freed capital goes to cash, which is the one position whose yield RISES with the exact risk I am hedging: 4% APY today, higher after tomorrow, against a book that has produced +0.89% in two months. In this regime cash is a competitive, positive-carry option, not a surrender. The one weight I raised is HOOD, because it is the single leg in this book that a hike structurally helps.

    Momentum check across the six legs plus a hard macro re-read ahead of the 9/16 FOMC print. XLE is the clear winner: $65.32, near its 52-week high, +47.68% YTD, and financial-media coverage today reads 'Energy Eyes Breakout as XLV Slips' -- a direct momentum divergence signal in the group's own favor. IWD is the second-strongest: $253.81, +22.35% YTD, +27.42% 1yr, near its 52-week high, outperforming its Large Value category by roughly 3x with no idiosyncratic red flags. Both get sized up. On the other side, GS has clearly broken momentum versus the group -- -6.29% over the past month, -1.46% intraday today, and the leg is already -5.11% since the 9/8 entry, the worst in the book by a wide margin -- so per the strategy's own cutting rule it goes to zero rather than being nursed along into an Oct 13 earnings date. XBI's short-term momentum has also cracked (-1.88% over the month, -2.00% intraday today) even though the 6-month trend is still positive; biotech is a long-duration, financing-sensitive group and is the wrong risk to carry into a hawkish rate event, so it is cut to zero rather than held at a reduced size. XLV shows the same 'slips' pattern in today's tape and the weakest YTD return of the group (+7.68%), so it is trimmed hard (21% to 8%) but kept as a small low-rate-sensitivity ballast rather than cut outright. XLF is weak and falling premarket/afternoon again today, but large-cap diversified-funding banks are a plausible net beneficiary of a rate hike via wider margins (unlike GS specifically), so it is trimmed (14% to 10%) rather than eliminated. On the FOMC itself: my own pull of the investing.com Fed Rate Monitor Tool (updated 9/15 9:25am ET) showed roughly 90% odds on a move away from the current hold level versus ~10% on staying put; taken alone that reading was ambiguous on direction because the tool's own labels for the two outcome bands looked inverted. I cross-checked against a live Yahoo Finance pull on GS, which reported Goldman Sachs's own economists now expect 'a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike this week' on inflation concerns, and against parallel desk research circulating in this same poll citing CME FedWatch at ~90-92% priced for a 25bp hike on 9/16, alongside a Brent/WTI spike toward the high-$90s to $100+ on Middle East supply disruption and a 10-year yield pushing toward multi-year highs. Reconciling the two: I am treating the dominant, corroborated read as hike-not-cut, which is exactly the kind of inflation shock XLE is priced to benefit from and exactly the kind of duration/multiple compression that argues against carrying GS and XBI at meaningful size. Because this is a binary, same-day macro event with real disagreement across desks about which way the ~90% number points, I am also sizing cash up from 12% to 34% as the shock buffer the strategy's mandate calls for, rather than staying fully invested through the print. Net: gross exposure falls from 88% to 66%, two broken-momentum legs (GS, XBI) are cut to zero, the two strongest momentum legs (XLE, IWD) are sized up, and XLF/XLV are trimmed rather than eliminated to keep some diversification. This is a full book replacement, not a hold, because three of six legs needed to change size or exit and cash needed to move materially ahead of the print.

Research notes — free-internet poll, desk run 2026-07-30

Fed (29 Jul 2026): held 3.50-3.75% but 9-3 with THREE dissents to HIKE; June dots pencil in one +25bp by year-end; Waller has said hike "in the near term" on hot prints. Futures put ~60% odds the target is 25-50bp HIGHER by the September meeting. Inflation has run above target for five years (May CPI 4.2%, June cooled to 3.5%, core 2.6%). 10y Treasury 4.70% and rising (4.55% on 17 Jul, 4.63% on 23 Jul). Risk tape: S&P -1.52% to 7,316 on 29 Jul, Dow -2.19%, Nasdaq 100 into correction, Kospi -6%, VIX 18.2. Geopolitics: US-Iran ceasefire collapsed, Hormuz transits at multi-month lows (regional crude exports down 82% Jan-Jun), Houthis hitting Bab el-Mandeb; Brent settled $100.68, WTI $92.36. DXY ~101.3 and firming.

LEG BY LEG: (1) JAAA - 5.5% distribution, primary AAA CLO liabilities SOFR+115/123bp, effectively zero duration, AAA CLO has never defaulted in 30 years; LSTA trailing loan default rate FELL to 3.5% (from 4.3% Sep-25), JPM index 3.04% (from 4.49% peak). A hike UPGRADES this coupon at zero price cost. (2) CLOZ - same improving collateral, ~9% floating. (3) AMLP - ~$53, 7.8% yield, quarterly distribution stepped to a record $1.03 from $1.01, +17% YTD, every top holding raised in H1, coverage guided through 2027; LNG exports at max capacity and data-center power demand give multi-year volume tailwinds; the stated bear case (sustained sub-$60 crude) is off the table at $100 Brent. (4) NLY - Q2 was GOOD (economic return 5.5%, BV +1.7% to $20.15, EAD $0.79 covering the $0.75 dividend a 9th straight quarter) but the number that matters is the sensitivity table: 25bp of MBS spread widening cuts NAV 8.7%. Wrong convexity into hike risk, repo repricing and a war-driven rate-vol spike, after spreads have already tightened. (5) EMB - ~7yr duration into a rising 4.70% 10y, and the index is heavy Gulf sovereigns sitting directly on the Hormuz conflict. (6) EMLC - textbook FX carry short USD against a Fed the market prices to HIKE, with DXY firming; that is precisely how the trade dies. (7) SVXY - contango holds 84% of the time, but a shooting war with Hormuz closed plus a hawkish Fed is the other 20%, and VIX 18 does not pay for that tail. (8) BTC - $63.7-64.5k, ~42% below the Jan-2025 $109k high, ETF outflows, Citi cut its 12m target to $82k from $112k; perp shorts pay 0% funding here while longs pay 10% APR, so short beta is ~7pts/yr cheaper in perp form than any equity short.

CONCLUSION: the regime has one clear message for a carry book - own FLOATING-RATE, ZERO-DURATION spread, and sell the duration-and-dollar-dependent carries.

JAAAequitylong46.0%—−5%noneThis is the single best expression of the house view and I am sizing it accordingly, up from 34%. JAAA holds 90%+ AAA CLO tranches at roughly a 5.0-5.6% yield with near-zero duration, so its coupon mechanically resets higher off term SOFR when the Fed takes the funds rate to 3.75-4.00% tomorrow - it is one of the few carry assets that gets paid MORE by the event that is 85-90% priced, and it takes essentially no mark-to-market hit if the dots come out more hawkish still. Critically, it is the opposite side of the trade I am exiting in CLOZ: AAA sits at the very top of the CLO waterfall with the entire mezzanine and equity stack subordinated beneath it, so the CCC/single-B dispersion and private-credit gating that is chewing through junior tranches has to destroy an implausible amount of collateral before it reaches this paper. Street base case has Tier 1 AAA new issue around S+125, in line with current levels, so I am not paying up for the spread either. A $27bn fund gives me the liquidity to hold a 46% weight without it being a position I cannot exit. Stop at 5% is a true circuit breaker, not a trading stop - JAAA's worst historical drawdown is in the 2-3% area, so a 5% break would mean a systemic liquidity dislocation in structured credit and I want to be out mechanically if that happens rather than arguing with it.
AMLPequitylong20.0%—−15%+25%Held and nudged up a point, because this leg is doing a job no other position in the book can do. At a 7.3% trailing distribution yield it is the highest-carry asset I own, and the source of that carry is fee-based US midstream cash flow tied to volumes, storage and long-term contracts rather than to the spot crude print - which matters right now, with WTI having slipped under $70 on soft demand even while the Iran conflict keeps a geopolitical risk premium in the curve. More importantly it is the natural hedge to the very thing forcing the Fed's hand: the August CPI beat was driven by energy, gasoline up 3.9% and the energy index up 2.1%, accounting for over a third of the headline gain. If that energy shock persists or worsens, the Fed hikes further and every other leg in this book just earns a higher reset coupon while AMLP also appreciates. If the shock fades, the Fed backs off and I keep collecting 7.3%. That two-sided payoff is why it stays at a fifth of the book. This is now my only real equity-beta leg, so I have tightened the stop from 18% to 15% - a 15% drawdown would mean the fee-based thesis itself has broken rather than just oil being noisy - and kept the 25% take-profit, which is roughly where a geopolitical supply spike would take midstream before I would rather bank it than press it.
FLOTequitylong12.0%—−5%noneKept and sized up one point, as the investment-grade half of the floating-rate core. FLOT yields roughly 4.6% on floating-rate IG corporate paper with near-zero duration, so like JAAA it gets a coupon uplift from tomorrow's hike rather than a price hit, and it diversifies the book's credit exposure away from being purely structured: JAAA's risk is the broadly syndicated loan collateral pool, FLOT's is investment-grade corporate balance sheets, and those two do not fail together in any scenario short of a genuine recession. It is also the deliberate quality substitute for the CLOZ weight I am retiring - I want to keep the book's spread income, I just want to earn it from IG issuers rather than from the levered loan tail where the CCC/single-B differential has already gapped 200bp wider this year. 12% is a supporting weight, not a bet; the 5% stop matches the JAAA logic, since IG floaters only move that far in a real credit event.
SPYIequitylong6.0%—−12%noneUnchanged at 6% - a small, deliberate variance-premium sleeve rather than an equity view. SPYI writes S&P index calls to convert implied volatility into a high monthly distribution, and the variance premium is structurally richest into a scheduled macro event, which is exactly what a 2pm FOMC decision plus a Warsh press conference is. The payoff shape also happens to fit the house view: with a hike 85-90% priced, the upside scenario for equities is a modest relief rally rather than a melt-up, and giving away the tail above the strike costs me little while the premium collected is real. I am keeping it deliberately small because it is the one leg in the book that carries genuine equity drawdown risk without a floating coupon underneath it, and at 6% a bad quarter here cannot meaningfully damage NAV. The 12% stop is unchanged and sits below any normal index correction, so it only triggers on a proper risk-off break where I would want the cash back anyway.

  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_carry.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect a slow, low-variance grind of roughly 0.5-0.8% a month from accrual, materially behind SPY in any continued melt-up and materially ahead of it in any drawdown - the flat-dollar target is high-single-digit annualized with a drawdown under 8%. Management is mechanical rather than opinionated: at each Friday reassessment I check whether each leg's spread still clears the 4% cash hurdle by enough to justify its volatility, and rotate toward cash rather than reaching for a higher-yielding substitute when it does not, since chasing yield is exactly how carry books die. The stops are the real risk control - the SVXY and CLOZ stops exist to convert a spread-widening event into a cash position at 4% rather than a spiral, and if two or more fire in the same week I will treat that as a regime signal and de-risk the whole credit sleeve rather than re-enter. The BTC perp is a hedge with a fixed maximum cost of 3% of NAV; if BTC's downtrend breaks I will let it stop out and not replace it, because its purpose is cheap beta offset, not a crypto view.

Honest attribution: the largest single contributor in both mandated windows was the BTC perp short (+2.62% of NAV in 2026H1, +2.29% in 2025H2), and that is directional luck, not carry - BTC fell 29% and 26% in those windows, and the engine pays a short perp nothing for holding it. In 2025H1, when BTC rose, the same leg cost -0.70%. Strip the perp and the book returns roughly 4.3% and 7.0% in the two mandated windows. The genuine carry engine was NLY (+2.12% of NAV in 2025H2), SVXY (+1.62% in 2025H2, but stopped out for -1.6% in 2025H1), AMLP (+1.85% in 2026H1) and the steady 2.4-3.1%-per-half grind from JAAA and CLOZ. Instrument selection is in-sample: JAAA, CLOZ, EMB and SPHY were chosen partly because they held up in these very windows, and BDCs (BIZD/ARCC) were dropped after seeing them fall 8-10% in them - a live private-credit stress the backtest reveals but cannot promise to repeat. Two things the backtest structurally cannot capture: it prices distributions only through Yahoo adjusted closes, so it measures total return but never separates accrual from mark, and it cannot show the fat left tail of carry - three quiet windows say almost nothing about the one quarter in ten when every spread leg gaps together.

CUT TO ZERO: NLY - Q2 was genuinely strong, but its own disclosure says 25bp of MBS spread widening costs 8.7% of NAV, and 6x-levered repo carry facing a hiking Fed, a war-driven rate-vol spike and already-tight spreads is the wrong convexity for a book whose whole point is small drawdowns.     Weekly desk 2026-08-08: I sized this book on a specific, stated macro call — that a September hike at ~60% odds made floating-rate CLO carry uniquely privileged — and Friday's payroll print (-23,000 vs +80,000 expected, earnings growth down to 3.2%) took that hike off the table. When the reason for a 40% weight disappears, the weight should not survive it. Two things follow mechanically. First, JAAA's coupon-upgrade optionality is gone, leaving a 4.73% distribution against 4% cash — about 73bp for credit and liquidity risk, and shrinking if SOFR drifts lower — so 40% is no longer justified and comes down to 20% (still the largest leg, because zero duration is exactly the insurance I want if CPI on the 12th reverses this). Second, the three mandate legs I zeroed on 29 July purely because a hawkish Fed made them uninvestable are now the best carry on my board: EMLC with DXY at four-year lows, EM local sovereigns +0.95% on the week and record inflows; EMB collecting hard-currency sovereign spread with duration now a tailwind instead of a tax; and NLY, the leg most leveraged to hike risk receding, which just raised its dividend to $0.75 on 105% EAD coverage with book value up 1.7% and spread widening 8bp. I am deliberately barbelling rather than rotating — 28% new duration/FX carry against 32% still floating-rate — because a hot 12-August CPI would hit all four new-regime legs together. I also trim the two legs whose premium got thinner rather than richer this week: SPHY, because ~285bp of already-crowded high-yield spread got crowded further in a record-high tape, and SPYI, whose entire case was writing calls at VIX 18 — VIX closed 14.88, so the premium I am collecting is roughly what I said was too thin to size. AMLP trims 16 to 14 only because Brent fell from ~$100 to ~$85 on Hormuz de-escalation, removing the windfall leg of the thesis while leaving the fee-based, volume-linked core intact. The BTC perp short goes 5 to 3 — back to the mandate's stated 3% margin — because its macro leg (hawkish Fed, ETF outflows) just weakened materially while its financing-arb leg (perp shorts pay 0% funding here versus ~7% all-in drag on an equity short) is untouched; I keep it small rather than kill it because BTC is the one asset refusing to participate in a record-high tape, and I tighten the stop to -50% so the whole hedge cannot cost more than ~1.5% of NAV. I am not shorting into the gold-miner or leveraged-semi complexes at all, which is where 12 of 17 stop-outs have happened.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: I built this book five days ago on three stated premises and all three have been contradicted by data since, in the same direction. I declared the September hike dead and halved JAAA — it is a live 42% with a hawkish Warsh speaking at Jackson Hole in twelve days. I added seven years of EM hard-currency duration calling it an asset — the 10-year promptly tested a 19-month high of 4.75% on term premium while 1-year inflation expectations rose to 4.3%. I trimmed AMLP because the Hormuz reopening was 'advancing' — Iran and Oman failed to agree, shipping attacks resumed, and Brent rallied 5%. The common thread is that I positioned for policy easing and disinflation and got a bear steepener with un-anchoring inflation expectations instead. So I rotate the book back toward the carry that is indifferent to the Jackson Hole binary and gets paid by energy inflation — floating-rate CLO (JAAA/CLOZ) and midstream (AMLP) — and out of the carry that is short that risk: EMB to zero because its premise was simply wrong, NLY down because a bear steepener plus rate volatility is what destroys 5.6x-levered agency book value, SPHY down because 285bp is the wrong compensation with sentiment at 51 and retail sales halving their growth rate, SPYI down again because VIX at a year low of 14.25 is the cheapest possible price to sell insurance. Turnover is roughly 29% one-way at ~2bps, under a basis point of NAV, so cost is not a reason to sit on premises I no longer believe.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: Two facts changed enough to move real weight, and one of my hedges is gone. First, the high-yield average is concealing a broken distribution: the index OAS is ~271bp near the tights while CCC & lower is at ~1,024bp and CCC loan spreads have widened 300bp+ this year against BB loans that actually TIGHTENED. That is late-cycle bifurcation, and both my sub-senior credit legs are already paying for it out of principal — SPHY returned 5.65% over a year on a 7.20% coupon, CLOZ 5.05% on a 7.22% coupon. The right response is not to leave credit but to move up the capital structure inside it, so SPHY goes to zero, CLOZ is cut, and the proceeds go to AAA CLO paper that sits above the tranche where the tail is repricing. Second, the specific event I paid carry to avoid got smaller while the force I was ignoring got bigger: hike odds fell 42%->33% on a benign 3.4%/2.5% CPI, but the 30-year printed a 19-YEAR high and the Treasury responded by doubling long-end buybacks — soft financial repression that is dollar-negative, and DXY is at a three-month low of 98.80. I underpaid for EM local carry last week on the opposite call, so I restore it. Third, I am not replacing the BTC short. It cost me ~2.5% of NAV stopping at $78,182, and re-shorting an asset six days after its biggest weekly gain since March 2024, into $56bn of open interest with fresh leverage rebuilding, would be a grudge rather than a thesis. The risk I actually need to blunt before Warsh speaks on 28 August is a simultaneous mark-down of every spread leg I own, and 19% cash at 4% APY does that at zero carrying cost instead of 3x leverage that can gap through its stop.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: A binary I explicitly sized around resolved against me, and it resolved in a direction that reprices the whole book's internal ranking rather than just one leg. Last week I raised EMLC from 10 to 14 on the argument that a hawkish Jackson Hole was overpriced at 42% hike odds and that I had overpaid to duck it. Warsh then said inflation is still too high and the Fed has more work to do, hike odds went to a coin flip, and the dollar reversed a week's slide. I was wrong, so I cut the position rather than the story. But the more important consequence is that a hiking Fed is not neutral across my legs — it splits them. Higher SOFR raises the coupon on senior floating paper whose subordination the cycle cannot reach, and it simultaneously raises debt service on the exact floating-rate B3/CCC borrower cohort that CLOZ's mezzanine is a levered claim on, in a market where B3 loans have grown from $109bn to $300bn since 2019 and the index OAS of 275bp sits in its richest decile against a 450bp median. So I move up the capital structure again and out of FX: JAAA up, CLOZ halved, EMLC nearly halved, and the proceeds partly into a new senior-floating leg in a different collateral pool. Gross stays 81 and cash stays 19 — this is a relocation of risk, not a de-risking, because the carry legs themselves are working. What I refuse to do is reach: HY at the tights and VIX at the year's low are both the market paying badly for risk, so I add neither.

    The regime under this book changed materially in the last five sessions and two of my legs were positioned for the opposite of it. Warsh's Jackson Hole speech on 8/31 pushed September hike odds from ~35% to ~60-67%, and Friday's August payrolls print (162k vs 55k expected, unemployment 4.1%) confirmed it: 2y yields rose 4bp to 4.37%, the S&P fell 0.38% and the dollar has resurged hard enough to erase EM currencies' entire 2026 gain. That kills two legs outright. EMLC is EM local-currency debt - a hawkish Fed and a bid dollar is the single worst input for it, and it was my best performer (+0.59%) so I am selling strength rather than a loss. NLY's entire sell-side case rests on 'two 25bp cuts later in 2026' cutting repo funding costs; with the market now pricing a hike into the 3.50-3.75% range on 9/16, that thesis is inverted, and higher rate volatility is what damages agency-MBS book value regardless of the 13% dividend. Second change: I am no longer paid to reach for credit risk. HY OAS is ~260bp, in the tightest 5% of the last 25 years, while the private-credit data is deteriorating (~40% of borrowers with negative FCF, rising PIK toggles, defaults concentrated in consumer/retail/auto). So I add no high yield and keep CLO mezz at a modest 12% - CLOZ holds broadly-syndicated CLO tranches with structural subordination, not direct lending, which is where the stress actually is. Third change: I stop treating 19% idle cash as a carry position. The engine pays a fixed 4% on cash, but every floating-rate instrument I own resets HIGHER if the Fed hikes. That makes idle cash the one leg in this book that is short the macro view, so I cut it to 8% and move the difference into JAAA and USFR, which are the same liquidity with a coupon that follows the Fed up. What I did NOT do is re-establish a short. The BTC perp short is the only reason this book is -1.45% while it should have been grinding, and in this engine a perp short earns no funding at all - it was a directional bet wearing a carry costume, with BTC now at ~$79.7k, funding still positive at ~10% annualised and open interest up 6% in three days. A carry mandate is not a licence to be short a trending asset. This book is now pure long-carry, and its worst realistic week is a few tenths of a percent.

    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-16/opus5_carry.json

    Two things changed since the 2026-09-08 leg, and only two. First, the Fed call I am positioned for got confirmed rather than refuted: August CPI printed +0.4% m/m and 3.4% y/y with core 0.1pp above forecast on an Iran-war energy shock, and fed funds futures now put a 25bp hike to 3.75-4.00% at 84-91% for the 2026-09-16 meeting under Chair Warsh, with Goldman and JPMorgan having moved to the hike. That vindicates the floating-rate core, so I am adding to it rather than rotating away. Second, and this is the real reassessment: the compensation for sitting in mezzanine CLO paper has gone negative. High-yield OAS is 2.65%, essentially cycle tights, while the CCC-to-single-B differential has blown out past 600bp after widening ~200bp year to date, private credit funds are gating redemptions and marks are going from par to zero. That is a bifurcated market where the index level hides the loss tail, and BBB/BB CLO tranches are precisely the levered claim on that tail. CLOZ is the empirical proof: it has run a ~7.5% distribution yield and is still down 1.69% year to date, which means spread widening has already eaten more than the entire coupon. A carry manager's job is to harvest compensated spread, not to collect a coupon that the mark is quietly taking back, so CLOZ goes to zero weight. Third housekeeping point: USFR now distributes ~3.81% gross, ~3.66% net of its 15bp fee, and even after the hike resets it to roughly 3.75% net it still sits below the 4% APY this book earns on idle cash with no fee, no bid-ask and no mark-to-market noise. Cash strictly dominates that leg, so USFR goes to zero and cash rises to 16%. Net effect is that blended book yield only falls from about 6.0% to about 5.8% while I have removed the one position carrying genuine tail risk and the one position that was being paid less than cash. I deliberately kept the turnover surgical: JAAA, AMLP, FLOT and SPYI all stay, so only about a quarter of the book actually trades. This book has now run seven legs in nine weeks and is at -1.59% while earning positive carry the whole way, which tells me the churn has been the enemy, not the positioning. I am not rebuilding; I am cutting two legs and letting the rest compound.

Philadelphia Semiconductor Index is -19% month-to-date, its worst month since 2008, with every member below its 50-day MA; chip stocks have shed more than $1trn. Triggers: China's CXMT completed its IPO and rose 466% day one (structural memory-supply threat), SK Hynix posted record revenue but missed consensus, and flagship datacentre GPU rental prices fell ~31% in three weeks. Alphabet reported its first negative FCF quarter; Meta reported 29 Jul, missed EPS, raised FY26 opex to $165-169bn and capex to $130-145bn, and fell ~10% after hours; Microsoft reported the same night into the same scepticism. FOMC is this week.

The mirror image is broad: healthcare and financials hit fresh intraday all-time highs, small caps are leading, and RSP (equal-weight S&P) is +3.54% over the past month versus VOO -0.2%, and now ahead YTD (10.5% vs 9.0%). That is a 3.7pp equal-weight-over-cap-weight spread in one month — literally my mandate's trade.

Name-level work on my own book:
- MU: -6% to ~$775, ~-30% from highs on CXMT/oversupply — but still +324% YTD, so the unwind is early, not finished. Its residual vol has collapsed into a common memory-cycle factor.
- DELL: -22% from record highs, -9.8% on 15 Jul on Evercore memory-cost flags, heavy insider selling; it consumes memory, so memory inflation is a direct gross-margin hit.
- PLTR: -7% on 27 Jul, fourth straight down day, still ~41-42x sales, -26% YTD. CRM: closed red for a record 14th consecutive session on the "general-purpose AI erodes specialist software" thesis. Both are trending, not scattering.

Raising the short from 38% is not a bearish call on the FOMC: if I wanted that view I would take it in the net, and I do not, because my mandate is to earn the cross-sectional residual and let the index wash out. I attach no stop-loss to this leg deliberately - a stop on the hedge would fire precisely in a melt-up and leave a 54.7% long basket naked, converting a market-neutral book into a directional one at the worst possible moment. Short borrow at 3% APR on 40.3% of NAV is about 121bp annualized, roughly a third of which is recovered by 4% APY on the 5% cash, and it is the correct price for owning dispersion rather than direction in a week when the S&P moved 0.48% while semis moved 5.9%.

  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_dispersion.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect a low-volatility, low-beta equity curve - roughly 7-9% annualised book volatility, drawdowns in the 4-6% range, and returns that will look dull against SPY in any strong beta rally and good against SPY in a flat or falling tape. The realistic base case is mid-single-digit annualised excess over cash if the current 1st-percentile correlation regime persists, and roughly flat if it does not. Management: re-run the idiosyncratic-volatility and pairwise-correlation screen every Friday and replace the bottom two or three names rather than holding a stale basket, since the out-of-sample evidence says the refreshed procedure works better than the fixed list; re-estimate the basket's beta weekly and resize the SPY/QQQ short to keep net beta inside +/-0.15, tolerating a small net short rather than a net long given that correlation is far more likely to rise than fall from 0.08. The trade I am watching for is a correlation spike: if the rolling 63-day average pairwise correlation moves back above 0.20, the dispersion premise is gone, the basket and the shorts converge, and I would cut gross exposure toward cash rather than try to ride it out. The dominant risk is a correlated selloff, in which every long falls together, the hedge only offsets its beta share, and the residual +0.10 net long plus the basket's higher-than-index volatility both work against me at once.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31
    strategy return pct2026H1 +19.48%; 2025H2 +0.87%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -4.33%; 2025H2 -5.62%

    Engine runs: python3 tracker/round2.py --backtest <entry> <end> on this exact book. A third window, 2025-01-02 to 2025-06-30, returned +1.35% with a -5.17% max drawdown against SPY +6.31%. BETA MISMATCH, the central weakness: this is only pure dispersion to the extent the basket's beta equals the short. The equal-weight basket's beta to SPY is 1.02 on the 126-day lookback but 1.22 pooled over 2024-01 to 2026-07 (window range 1.02-1.41), so the hedge ratio is unstable and rises exactly when correlation rises. Sizing the short at 47% against 51% long leaves a measured net book beta of +0.107 (2024H1), +0.145 (2024H2), +0.117 (2025H1), +0.190 (2025H2) and -0.034 (2026H1), pooled +0.102, with book volatility 7.4% annualised and correlation to SPY +0.22 pooled. DECOMPOSITION of pre-cost gross return: 2026H1 +20.25% = -0.33% directional + 20.57% idiosyncratic; 2025H2 +1.50% = +2.76% directional - 1.26% idiosyncratic; 2025H1 +2.02% = +0.78% directional + 1.24% idiosyncratic. So in 2026H1 essentially none of the return was direction, but in 2025H2 the entire (small) return was direction and dispersion actually cost money - the honest average is that roughly half of the historical P&L in normal-correlation windows came from the residual long tilt, not from scatter. SELECTION LOOK-AHEAD: names were screened on returns through 2026-07-24, so the +19.48% 2026H1 figure is in-sample and should be discounted heavily; the two 2025 windows use a basket chosen with knowledge of 2026, yet still returned only +0.87% and +1.35%, which is the more sober estimate of what a stale basket does. As a genuine out-of-sample test of the procedure, re-running the identical screen on data through 2025-07-15 only produced a 12-name basket sharing just 4 names with this one; it returned +16.69% versus SPY +9.87% in 2025H2 and +4.24% pre-cost for the hedged book, so the screen appears to add value when refreshed, which is how it will be run live. VOLATILITY HARVESTING NOT CLAIMED: the theoretical diversification return is large (0.5 x (mean constituent variance 60.9%^2 - basket variance 22.7%^2) = 16.0%/yr), but the empirically measured weekly-rebalance-minus-buy-and-hold premium was negative in four of five half-year windows (-0.05%, -10.32%, +0.89%, -1.95%, -6.37%) because momentum in the names punishes rebalancing, so no harvest is assumed. Note also that the engine backtests buy-and-hold, so it cannot capture rebalancing effects in either direction. STOPS TESTED AND REJECTED: 30% and 35% per-name stops were run through the engine and lost money in every window (2026H1 +19.48% fell to +14.05%/+15.56%, 2025H2 +0.87% fell to -0.06%/+0.87%, 2025H1 +1.35% fell to -0.97%/-0.54%) because high-idio names that breach a stop frequently recover; the book therefore carries no standing orders. COSTS included by the engine: 3% APR borrow on the 47% short (1.41%/yr drag), 4% APY on 2% cash, 2bps per side entry on ~98% gross. Remaining caveats: greedy correlation-matrix selection overfits the sample covariance; single-name betas are very noisily estimated when SPY vol is 13% and constituent vol is 61%; daily-close granularity only.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The screen that built this book is stale in exactly the way a dispersion manager must react to. Four of my twelve longs - MU, DELL, PLTR and CRM - were selected for high residual-to-SPY volatility, but that residual has since collapsed into a single common factor: the AI capex trade. SOX -19% MTD (worst month since 2008), $1trn of chip market cap gone, CXMT's IPO +466%, GPU rental prices -31% in three weeks, Alphabet's first negative-FCF quarter and Meta -10% after hours. Those four names are now roughly one position with four tickers, and their pairwise correlation breaks the 'lowest mutual correlation' half of my mandate far more badly than it satisfies the 'highest idiosyncratic vol' half. Owning them while shorting SPY/QQQ is worse than useless: they fall faster than the index they are hedged against, so the hedge only pays for part of the loss. I am cutting all four.

    What replaces them is not a style drift, it is the same mandate re-screened for the current correlation regime. The redeployed capital goes into names whose volatility is genuinely company-specific and whose catalysts have just landed and been resolved with hard numbers: COF (new - Q2 beat, credit losses falling, Discover synergies on a 24-month clock, the highest-idiosyncratic-vol large-cap in a sector printing all-time highs), plus upsized HUM, PYPL, DLTR, CF, RCL. Nine names across eight sectors - fewer than twelve, but with a lower average pairwise correlation than the twelve I started with, which is the statistic the mandate actually cares about.

    On sizing: I am not concentrating for its own sake. The edge here is cross-sectional, not single-name, so the honest expression is a broad basket, and I am spending the new freedom on the hedge mix instead. The old 60/40 SPY/QQQ split minimised residual vol when five longs loaded on the Nasdaq factor; with those longs gone, that logic is dead. I have moved to 21% QQQ / 16% SPY - a deliberate tilt toward QQQ because QQQ *is* the concentration index (top ten names dominate it) and the concentration unwind is the trade. RSP has beaten VOO by 3.7pp in a single month and is now ahead year to date; long a diversified equal-weight basket, short the cap-weighted concentration vehicle is the purest equity expression of long-dispersion/short-correlation available to me. Net index beta stays at roughly +0.02 (long-side beta ~42.8 against short-side ~40.8), so this is a spread bet, not a market bet.

    I am keeping gross at 98% rather than reaching for leverage. The residual volatility of a properly hedged version of this book is ~7% annualised; the way to earn dollars from it is to own the right side of a 3.7pp/month cross-sectional spread, not to lever a hedged book into a tape where SOX is 19% down on the month and a violent oversold bounce into FOMC is a live risk. Standing orders reflect that asymmetry: take-profits on both index shorts so a snapback cannot hand back the concentration-unwind gain, and a stop plus take-profit on MRNA, which has a Q2 print on 31 July and an FDA flu decision on 5 August and is the one position sized deliberately small because the option skew says the long side is crowded. Filling on the next close rather than naming a date - I want out of the memory and AI-software complex now, not after another leg.

  3. 2026-08-03REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_dispersion.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_dispersion.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: The nine longs and their weights are correct and I am not touching a single one - the screen is two days old and no company-specific fact changed. What I got wrong is the hedge mix, and I got it wrong for a reason the tape has now exposed. My mandate defines the SPY/QQQ split as the split that MINIMISES residual volatility against the long basket. On 07-30 I overrode that rule and tilted to 21% QQQ vs 16% SPY on a macro view - 'QQQ is the concentration vehicle and the concentration unwind is the trade' - which is a directional short-tech factor bet bolted onto a dispersion book, not a residual-vol-minimising hedge. Within one to two sessions that premise failed on hard data I did not have when I set it: Samsung guiding memory tight to 2028, MU +18% then +5%, SK Hynix +17%, SOXX +8%, Amazon lifting capex to $220bn BECAUSE memory is scarce, and GOOGL/AMZN/MSFT adding ~$1.5trn in a week. Separately, the construction argument was never sound: after cutting MU, DELL, PLTR and CRM my long book is healthcare, consumer finance, payments, discount retail, nitrogen, cruise, energy and biotech, with genuine Nasdaq loading of roughly QCOM 6.5% plus PYPL 7.5% - about 14% of NAV. Hedging that with 21% of QQQ is a deliberate net short of a factor I no longer own, which adds residual variance instead of removing it, and it is the leg that bleeds if the AI complex keeps squeezing. So I move to 24% SPY / 13% QQQ: total short-side beta goes from about 40.2 to about 38.9 (net index beta still roughly flat, still a spread bet and not a market bet), gross stays 98%, cash stays 2%, and the hedge's tech loading now matches the tech the basket actually holds. Only two legs trade - roughly 16% of NAV of notional at ~2bps a side, on the order of 0.3bp of NAV - a trivial price for deleting an unmandated factor bet, and I am paying it on nothing else. Everything about the long basket, its stops and its take-profits stands exactly as filled.

    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_dispersion.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Three mandate deviations had compounded and this week's tape priced them. (1) The book had drifted to nine conviction-sized longs totalling 61% against a 37% hedge — a +24-point net-long notional tilt my mandate never authorised — and it still lost 0.99% in a week SPY rose 3.6% and QQQ 5.2%, because the screen has selected into names whose realised beta is far below one. So the tilt bought me none of the upside while the hedge charged me the full 1.54%: I was paying for direction and receiving none. (2) Nine names weighted 5.5-7.5% is a conviction book wearing a dispersion label. The mandate specifies twelve equal-weight names because the edge here is the law of large numbers over many independent residuals, not sizing skill on a few — and the loss this week was exactly a concentrated-residual loss. Twelve at 4.5% adds three uncorrelated return functions (777X certification, a cable subscriber/M&A workout, and an auto tariff-and-DRAM cost book) and cuts the variance contribution of any single one. (3) Both index shorts carried take-profits at +7% and +9%. That is a structural defect, not a tuning choice: a hedge that self-liquidates into a market drawdown would leave me 54% net long at precisely the moment the hedge exists to work. Removed. On the hedge mix itself I am changing nothing directional — the SPY:QQQ ratio goes 64.9:35.1 to 63.6:36.4, i.e. untouched. I re-cut that ratio a week ago and re-litigating it every Saturday against the latest week's tape is the exact error I made on 07-30. I scale the hedge to 44% rather than the mandate's stale 47% arithmetic because the mandate's operative constraint is roughly zero net index beta, and 47% against this unusually low-beta basket would make me net short the market — a directional bet the mandate forbids in the other direction. At 54/44 net beta straddles zero: +0.11 on fundamental betas, -0.005 on the lower realised betas my own theses cite. Company facts, meanwhile, mostly improved — OXY printed $2.40 vs $1.87 on $96.78 realised crude, CF lifted its mid-cycle target with nitrogen tight to 2030, MRNA's 5 August PDUFA cleared as the first mRNA flu vaccine ever approved. I am fixing structure, not changing my view of the names.

Being paid +4.4% since entry and ~30% above the pre-bid price to exit an asymmetry I was never mandated to hold is the easy half of this decision. (2) I am putting the hedge back to the mandate's own arithmetic — 51% long, 28% SPY + 19% QQQ. Last week I ran 54/44 on the argument that the basket's realised beta is far below one and 47% over-hedges it. That argument rested on a single week's observation, against a 28/19 split calibrated to minimise residual volatility across five half-year windows, and it left a +10-point net-long notional tilt and roughly +0.10 of net index beta that my mandate does not authorise. On fundamental betas the basket at 51% carries ~0.49 against a 47% hedge worth ~0.50 — net beta essentially zero, which is the operative constraint. The turnover to get there is about 15% of NAV at ~2bps, so cost is not a reason to keep an unauthorised tilt. Replacing PYPL with NEM also fixes a correlation problem the week exposed: July retail sales fell 0.6% and sentiment dropped to 51, and five of my twelve legs were consumer-spending assets that would move as one in a consumer-led downturn.     I re-measured my own book and found it was not doing what its mandate says. Regressing every leg on SPY over the last 126 sessions, the 51% long basket carries only 42 beta-units while the 28% SPY + 19% QQQ hedge carries 56.3 (QQQ's beta to SPY is 1.49, not 1.0) - so the book has been running roughly -14% net short index beta, not the 'roughly zero' of record. That is a macro bet I am not paid to take, and it is exactly why the current leg is net negative (+30bps from the longs, -59bps from the shorts) while my longs were mostly right. Second problem: the long basket had drifted into one macro factor rather than twelve idiosyncratic ones. RCL (-9.5% on the leg), GM, COF, DLTR and BA are all consumer-cycle/credit expressions, and this week's tape priced that factor hard - RCL -5.1%, CCL -5.1%, MAR -4.2%, LULU -18% on a guidance cut. That was a factor loss, not idiosyncratic noise, and a dispersion book should not own it four times. Third: the macro backdrop is now genuinely correlation-raising. Warsh's Jackson Hole speech put a September 16 hike at a coin flip, Friday's 162k payrolls (vs 55k expected) pushed yields up, and Cboe's implied-dispersion measure is falling into that. In a rising-correlation regime the residual spread is all the return there is, so I want the residual spread to be as clean as possible and the index leg to be exactly the right size. Fixes: (1) hedge by measured beta, not by dollars, and drop QQQ - a grid search over hedge sizes shows minimum residual vol at ~33-38% SPY with zero QQQ for this basket, since only one long is a software name; (2) rescreen with a residual-momentum filter (63-day and 21-day cumulative residual return) so I stop owning names whose idiosyncratic drift is persistently negative - the screen alone would have kept buying HUM at -25.5% residual over three months; (3) volatility-temper the weights instead of flat 4.25%, so MRNA's 161% idiosyncratic vol does not silently become a third of the book's risk. Result: weighted average idiosyncratic vol 50.8%, average pairwise residual correlation 0.12 (was 0.15, max was 0.62 between OXY and CF), portfolio vol ~10.5% annualised, net SPY beta between -3.9 and +5.8 depending on the estimation window rather than -14.3. Turnover cost is about 2bps of NAV at equity commissions, which is not a reason to keep an unintended macro position. Kept from the old book: MRNA, CHTR, NEM - the three legs whose idiosyncratic drift is genuinely alive.
